full_text:
This interview began informally over lunch, so now background information is provided at the start of this transcription, which is the start of the formal interview.

Interviewer:	Are there any other placement students here? 

Subject:	[Name’s] here, she’s on the same course as me. IDT does exactly the same module as me, but she started two weeks later. Because originally they only took on one placement student and they decided to take on the second one because of the amount of interest. And, it’s interesting to see how [name] and I have adapted to being down here. Because I was on campus for the first two years and [name] lived at home in [town] with her parents. So, she’s er, she’s straight in there. You know, she’s missing her family but she seems to be doing fine. Whereas I’m really missing the Uni atmosphere and going into the department.

Interviewer:	Is it quite quiet down here?

Subject:	Yeah. Very quite. I mean it’s good in the office and I’ve settled in completely with all the lads and everything. But it’s a bit weird because all mainly there are three ladies who are engineers and the, all the other females staff are admin staff. So, it’s a bit of a divide. It’s taken me a while to be accepted, I think. And for them to try and work out what I can do. And they expect me to keep bursting into tears on site and stuff like that but, apart from that, it’s okay. 

Interviewer:	So, is there any particular reason why they wanted design students and not engineering students? 

Subject:	Well [name] that [name] mentioned was from our department, he’s a BA there. And his Aunty [name] works here. And she’s one of the engineers. So that’s how he got in and then they decided that they didn’t want another BA student, they wanted a BSc with the mechanics. But to be honest, I haven’t used it really so. 

Interviewer:	When do you make the decision, whether to do a BA or a BSc? 

Subject:	Erm in the middle of first year, half the way through so. The first year, you’ve got mechanics and electronics and materials which is all compulsory. And then once you’ve had your mid term exams, is when they start to look at whose going to carry on through or not. And whose more styling orientated. But I think styling’s boring. So, I decided to do mechanics. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that more girls do the BA? 

Subject:	Definitely. Definitely. Definitely because I mean not many do the BSc full stop. There’s about twenty in the mechanics class and the materials. But the materials is combined with Mech eng as well. But erm in mechanics there are four girls, sixteen lads. But, that’s what it’s like with most of our lessons anyway, so. (Yeah, that’s true) But it’s not too bad. But I’m used to that. I’m used to having more lads around than girls. And it seems strange if there’s more girls around. (Yeah) It’s okay but I’m quite outgoing, so. If I feel that anyone’s feeling awkward around me, or whatever, I’m more likely to talk about it and say, “Right you know, what’s your problem?” Rather than worrying about it and go all quite and shy. Which I thinks put a few of them. Well, shaken them up a bit and, but now they’ve accepted me. But, it’s hard going out here because there was lots of site works and I’ve been involved, [name] who you met, is the Head of the Northern Ireland team which I’ve been put into. And that’s now just finishing off, so, wherever they’re doing nights in Belfast. (Right) With armed police going passed in case of IRA bombings. And, going up and down really slope, steep embankments at the side of the bridges. And gale force winds and snow. And everything like that. 

Interviewer:	How long were you there for then?

Subject:	I’ve been out there eight times now, just for a week each time. So you stay in hotels over there with the drillers and whoever’s sub-contracted. And the engineers as well. And the first time it was very strange. It’s like being on holiday but not. (Yeah) With the really strong accents and everything, it’s you really clear you don’t fit in. But then, after that, still I think a lot of the guys, you know, they’re saying, “Are you okay doing this?” And I thought, well if he can do it, I can do, there’s no problem there. So it’s like, “Are you sure you’re okay?” And it’s just; it’s alright because there’s a tiny bit of sexism in there. And some of the things where they just don’t think. It’s like guys like, toilet facilities, wonderful, where erm you know obviously it’s easier for them just to jump into the back of the field at four o’clock in the morning. Whereas I’m like, erm no. You know I can’t do that. Yeah, and I’m still learning to drive, I’ve got my test at the end of March. So I’ve been learning whilst I’ve been down here and it’s a case of then me having to say so well look, you know, please can you direct me to the next service station? Because they’re all on the motorways anyway, on the bridges. And I’ll, oh you girl aargh. Well but, it depends. Like normally, it won’t bother me but four o’clock in the morning, you’re down there, shout, “Go away”. 

Interviewer:	Do they have porta-cabins or anything?

Subject:	Not at all. It’s take as little as you need over there basically. But, apart from that ...

Interviewer:	Do you have to wear safety clothing? 

Subject:	U-hum. 

Interviewer:	Clothing? 

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Does that fit you? 

Subject:	We’ve got all the PP. It’s like the standard Health and Safety stuff. 

Interviewer:	But is that all men’s sizes? 

Subject:	Yeah. And er you go through issues with the guys trying to kit you out. And because all the safety boots are in men sizes as well. So, I had to get a size five and I’m a size seven. And stuff like that but also the, the big yellow coats. Obviously, chest sizes appropriately. So, I now have, I’ve got massive a coat, but it fastens and its comfortable, you can move around and stuff. But, that doesn’t bother me. That side of me doesn’t really; I’m not too fussed about it, because it’s the same through DT, so I’m used to it now. 

Interviewer:	But is it right?

Subject:	It’s not right, no. But you know like everything fastens on the male side and everything. But when you’re out on site, and of course, there’s no make up, hair tired back. The hat pulled down, you know. And some of the guys go, “Oh God, you look different”. And I’m thinking erm, “thanks”, they wouldn’t say that if it was another bloke. And about, “Oh look at you all (inaudible) in your site jeans and everything”. “You look different”. I’m thinking well, I’m not going to wear this to work. And I’m not going to wear a suit on site, so. (Yeah. Well you wouldn’t…) Exactly. There are a couple of the comments where you just think, hmmm. 

Interviewer:	What proportion of your work is out on site then?

Subject:	Quite, quite a lot. It was initially. Now it’s about forty percent. But there’s [name] here as well, who’s one of the engineers, and she’s a tomboy. But she’s really, really nice. And she’s paved the way a lot and I was out on site with her, down in Cornwall for the first few times. And she basically toughened me up a bit and sort of sliding down erm slippery slopes and towards rivers. And you’re sliding down sloped towards motorways and stuff. And you get lorries beeping you when you’re out there. Because you’re a girl and you’ve got bunches or whatever. And erm at first I was a bit like, you know, what on earth is going on? Yeah. It’s just like, come on, you can’t do this when the lads are there. You’ve got to, you’ve got to toughen up. You’ve got to just take it on the chin, or else you’re not going to get anywhere. And if it wasn’t for her doing that then, I think things would be a lot different now. But, you get used to it now, you just laugh it off and if lorry drivers beep at you, and you, and you just like do the honking the horn back at them and. Just take it on the chin, because you’re going to get it wherever. I’m a lot more laid back about it now. It used to really annoy me. And in DT it used to annoy me. But now, when I first arrived, I was thinking “God, it’s followed through to the workplace now”. It’s the same, old boy, you know kind of logic to a lot of it. And [name]’s very heavily involved in the [name] Club. He’s the chairman. And I was invited along twice now. And I was the only woman in the room. And they were like accountants, engineers, doctors, policeman and everything. And they were all, you know, this is the placement student for engineering. And er one of them actually said, “But you’re a girl”. And I went, “Well spotted”. But, I don’t know. In a way, I’m. I used to see it as a bit of a disadvantage. But now I’m turning around as I am different, and I can communicate better than a bloke or most of them here anyway. And I’m confident. But at the same time, I can reach both males and females. I don’t have to, you know, try and tone down the language for anyone or anything like that, I’d just be straight me. And I’m fine. So, I’m seeing that more as a plus point than a downside. So, things are changing, definitely. 

Interviewer:	Ok, I’ll go through some of my questions then. Do you want to tell me a bit about [company] or do you want leave that for [name] to do? 
 
Subject:	You can have my interpretation of [company]. 

Interviewer:	Then I can compare them. 

Subject:	U-huh. [company] is a big American owned company. Head office is New York. (Right) So we don’t very often hear from New York to be honest. Erm when I first started here, I got the impression it was a smaller company. And I was amazed to found out, there were offices throughout all of the world basically. Europe, Asia etcetera, etcetera. Erm this particular [town] branch, upstairs is to do with structural engineering, civil engineering. Downstairs is to do with highways, traffic management, traffic counting. Highly exciting stuff. Upstairs is split into to SIG, which is the Structures Investigation Group, which I’m part of. Led by [name], [name] and [name] and then there’s the bridge designers. And then there are people who look at really severe problems in our little group. 

Interviewer:	Where are there other bases in the UK then?

Subject:	There are. There the head offices are in [town]. They keep calling it. Erm [town], [town]. Then the main one[town] as well. But there are lots of little sub-offices scattered throughout. And there are about four down this neck of the woods, [town] and [town] and here. (Oh) But, a lot of the offices are quite a stand alone. They don’t work so much with the other offices. But er it fiercely competitive. And everything is. 

Interviewer:	Competitive, within the organisation or what the organisation do is competitive?

Subject:	Both. Everybody’s on promotional run. And it’s a kind of atmosphere where anyone will work any overtime whatsoever to get a few brownie points. And I’m not in that frame of mind whatsoever so, but as far as I’d see, I’m placement student. I can’t be promoted. (Yeah) If I was, it would cause major tax issues. So, I don’t know. But there is a lot of stress and pressure about promotion and there’s a lot of erm bickering about the status and things like that. Going on, that I’m aware of round and about. But it’s quite; it’s a challenging atmosphere really. Because some of the things; you’ve got to; everything’s somebody says, you’ve got to take out the situation and think, right what do I know about this company or this person? And what they’re saying, are they likely to have said this? Or done that? Because everyone puts this slight slant on it to benefit themselves. Which I know is the business world and everything but. 

Interviewer:	Has that taken some getting used to?

Subject:	Um definitely. Because I’m used to just like at university, people saying like this is good, this is bad. You know, this is what this company does. You know and they give you a fair and unbiased, supposedly un-biased opinion. Whereas here, [company] are always the best. And, and it is good but there’s a lot of emphasis on training and the personal development, which is good. And a large IT support network, and everything like that. So there’s always somebody you can turn to. And erm like the HR Department and Public Relations to do with bullying and everything like that, which I have had experience of here. And it’s just; there are certain levels where there are all these supposed facilities that, you know people you can talk to, people who help you etcetera, etcetera. But there are limits and, I don’t know. 

Interviewer:	By that, do you mean that there are polices in place but in reality …

Subject:	It reality it doesn’t happen. (Yeah) Because there’s this entire three strike rule. The situation I was in, I may as well tell you, the guy whose in the kitchen, the blonde guy, [name] erm had issues with me about being a student. And erm the situation is [name] and I are writing our dissertations, basically regarding the development of equipment for site. There’s lots of time being wasted and the products are just like bricks and it’s awful. And ergonomically, I can’t hold it because it’s too deep for me. You have to hold it like that, but it’s so uncomfortable, whereas the guys you know, they’re all, alright. But yet again, it’s this, not catering for women whatsoever and everyone was saying, “Oh this is dreadful”. “And I wouldn’t design this”. But, you know, it was like, “Oh well, that’s engineering for you”, shrug of the shoulders. Erm but [name]’s taken a great dislike to the fact that, I’m saying things to [name], because I’ve learnt there’s a certain way to tackle things with [name]. And there’s certain steps you go through to get listened to. And you really do everything properly. Erm keep all your emails and remind him of stuff tactfully. I’ve learnt a lot of about diplomacy. Like that, and all the proper introducing people and keeping records of telephone calls, everything like that [name] really, really likes, he’s a very organised gentleman. So I’m in [name]’s good basically and [name]’s took a great disliked to me for that. And started calling me things like fucking bitch, in the workplace and erm the guys shrugged it off, because that’s what [name] is like. So I told [name]. [Name] is of the frame of mind that you can train anybody to do anything. And of course it looks bad on him if one of his members of staff are doing that, erm and this carried on for, this was about a couple of months ago. And this carried on for a couple of months. I thought, right this clearly, nothings happening. I told [name], I told [name] as well. [Name] sat and witness it. Didn’t to anything. And erm and [name] said well if you were a bloke, you’d just shrug your shoulders. And I’m like, “well, I’m not.” And this isn’t professional. I don’t care if they’re male or female, this isn’t professional in the workplace and I’m not being targeted because I’m female or because I’m a student or because I’m at university. Or anything like that, it’s just not on. And I think that took them all back a bit. Because then this initially quiet placement student has had enough. And I thought right, you know, I’m putting my foot down. And so I rang up [name] who’s one of the big bod’s in HR in [town] and she wasn’t having any of it. She was all for coming down here and meeting them and sorting them out and. Which is an amazing response compared to, what I’d had, just you know, keep a log of it. Which doesn’t do anything, and of course I get more tense and more sensitive as to everything he’s saying and doing. And it feels like everything he says is an attack on me, type of thing. And I was trying really hard not to, you know be like a typical prima-donna, and burst in tears or anything. But at the same time, I thought I’m not going to take it. I’m not willing to take it. And when [name], and when I spoke to [name] and told him I’d been in contact with HR and I had a erm a copy of the Grievance Policy. And I knew what my rights were. And if something wasn’t done, then I was going to follow this through with our without his support. (Yeah) Then [name] got called in. But this is months after, and he does it to everybody, but he’s particular focused on myself, [name] and [name]. And he’s still here. 

Interviewer:	That’s a coincidence, that you’re all women. 

Subject:	Yeah exactly. But I mean he’s been here two years now. And it’s on the grapevine. Everyone moans about it and everything. 

Interviewer:	But nothing ever gets done?

Subject:	No because you know he’s had his three strikes and supposedly out but he’s still here. And now, I actually said to him right outside. I thought if I can’t tackle you the proper way, I’m going to tackle you the male way. Like come outside and we’ll go talk about this. He’s like, “What?” You know like, right come on. And everyone’s like “Oh dear what’s she going to do?” And so, we’re outside, you know off the driveways, so its not company property. I said right, “What’s your problem with me? You’re not in work, no ones listening, what’s your problem with me?” And er he said, “You have greater earning potential than me.” 

Interviewer:	So basically, he’s just jealous?

Subject:	Yeah. Er well let’s go to uni then. It’s not my problem. It’s your problem. Deal with it. And walked back in. And he’s been fine with me now. But I shouldn’t have to take it that far. I mean things now are a lot better between us. Obviously, I’m still a bit a wary as to what’s going on and, if he really is genuine or if he’s still slagging me off or anything? But I don’t expect to be friends with everybody. 

Interviewer:	How did the other two girls react to that then? 

Subject:	 [Name], [name] just laughed it off, because [name]’s thirty. So she just use now. She goes home at the end of the day and that’s just work and whatever. And he’s just sad. [name], I think if affects [name] a lot more because [name]’s very quiet. And not being racist but I think that’s a cultural thing as well. You know she’s, she speaks when she’s spoken to. (Oh) And she greatly respects men and. (Yeah) A lot of the time, she’ll side on a man’s side even though, he can be blatantly wrong. And she doesn’t offer her own views or opinions. I mean to me, she says, rah rah rah, all these views and opinions and everything. But then, put her in a situation where there’s anybody on any level, and who’s male and she just won’t say it. So I think I’m now seen as the outspoken one. But, I’m not really. I used to be a lot more outspoken. I’m having to turn it down and keeping thinking well -

Interviewer:	Do you think what you have done has stopped him acting like that towards the other people or is he just better with you now?

Subject:	He’s just better with me now, he’s still the same with the others. (Yeah, yeah) But I basically; I told him straight. I said, “Well look I’ve been in contact with [name] who’s”, you know mentioned the name. And she’s quite fierce apparently, although I’ve never met her but apparently she’s quite fierce and very to the point. And erm I think then he realised I was taking it seriously. 

Interviewer:	That’s quite brave of you. 

Subject:	I just got. 

Interviewer:	Actually doing something about it.

Subject:	It got to the point though where; I mean I know [name] down here. I’ve made some friends through work but they’re work friends, they’re not friends. 

Interviewer:	Work colleagues?

Subject:	Exactly. And most of my friends are on placement this year. So I didn’t want to go back to university. It’s too late to do my final year anyway by then. And it got to the stage where I wasn’t looking forward to coming into work everyday. Not that many people do anyway. But, I really dreaded it. And when I was having my driving lessons, and I was having them straight after work, my driving instructor said, “Oh has [name] said something today then”, because, I was really tense and I was thinking at the end of the day, it came down to it, I felt I’m wasting money. Paying nineteen pound an hour for these driving lessons, if its going to take me half an hour for my driving instructor to keep pulling me over and telling me to calm down. And you’re thinking well, I’d just had enough. And it was the case of me moving, me quitting and going, or it being sorted. 

Interviewer:	Did you tell the university what was going on?

Subject:	I’ve told my placement tutor, [name]. 

Interviewer:	And was he supportive?

Subject:	Erm he’s very old school. He’s like [name]’s era. And he’s said, “Oh I think you’re probably being a bit hypersensitive” And this is all through emails. I was being very discrete about it and everything and erm because I said, you know, “He’s made some very offensive comments”. So I actually typed down to him everything that [name] said to me. So I have logged it down, it’s in my log book. Then he says, “Keep up a log book you know for you’re placement year, and I thought, right, you know, so I typed it all down. I said there are these ten cases, and I this is what he’s called me. And it’s all kinds of language and it’s all, a lot of it is female specific. And I says er, “Would you put up with that?” You know, because he’s got daughters. And I says, “If you daughter experience that at work, how would you feel?” And then, he became a lot more supportive. But beforehand, it was, “Er well you know some of the lads get abuse, and just take it because you’re a student”. But I’m not this year; I’m a member of this organisation. Which Donald sees and recognises but I think some of them do still see me as just a student, you know. But it’s interesting, but the first thing that [name] said on the phone was, “Would you like to transfer to Manchester?” “Because, because I’m from Preston so then I’d be closer to home, is it just that you’re homesick?” And I said, “No, because I’m staying here. If I can I’m staying here and I’m doing my time here because I’ve started here and I’m not a quitter. I’m not going to move. I’m not causing the problem”. And I’m not. You know so, I said if you want to move someone move him.

Interviewer:	So even she was a little bit ...

Subject:	And then when she saw I was digging my heels in, and she did the entire well you know, you may have to make the example of him and then, are you really willing to take the repercussions of this? I’m thinking well, but someone’s got to. Because, I’m going to be in a position, in a couple of weeks time where [placement tutor] emails me and says, “Do you feel this placement would be suitable for another student?” And [name]’s very keen for er the next student to be a girl as well, to keep the mix in the office, you know. And I was thinking I’m going to say no, at this stage, because I’m not going to put somebody else through this. (Yeah) And, you know, it goes through a phase of you know, you get chatted up initially, and then you’re mates and then you get the abuse . And it’s just not on, basically. But, I’m lucky in the fact that I’ve got a long term boyfriend. So, they’ve met each other. And he’s been backed off in that way as well. Whereas [name] isn’t in the same position. So she’s still a target. But, that’s up to her to do something. (Yeah) This year I’m, I used to take a lot on myself. I used to try to protect everybody within my social circle. And this year, it’s a case of right well, its dog eat dog, you look out for yourself. 

Interviewer:	Everyone for themselves? 

Subject:	And yet she doesn’t want do it. And I’m thinking, I can take it so far and say this, you know [name]’s well aware of what she’s experiencing, because I’ve told him. Erm but if she’s not willing to do anything about it, there’s nothing more I can do about it. (Yeah) So it’s not my problem. Which sounds harsh and my opinion would be the same if she was male or female. Because everyone else has to deal with it, so. 

Interviewer:	Did you meet the student who was here before? 

Subject:	 [Name], yes I did. Erm very loud, a bit of Casanova. Erm he, he seemed to get a long with everybody. He seemed like ideal as well really. But he did warn me about [name]. And he said not everybody erm, not the f - the face er, lots of people show you isn’t necessarily as they say, their true face, especially in the case of [name], so watch your back. And, at that time [name] was being absolutely charming with me. So I thought, what are you on about? You know, but, I was warned. But he’s younger, [name]’s younger sister’s here this year. Erm because she started at Loughborough but they put her down erm, what’s it called? Down near [name]. They put her in a mature student block, so she was the only fresher. (Oh no) Exactly. So, she didn’t get out in the fresher’s week and she didn’t enjoy it or anything. Because she doesn’t get to see, you know go into the uni or anything. You’re not going to go by yourself and things like that. So erm she left, so she’s down here for a year. And you can see it all over again, [name]’s trying to make a move on her. And she’s going to knock him back.

Interviewer:	So you can physically see happening, what happened to you?

Subject:	And now she’s say’s, you know his, she dumped her boyfriend, and it’s very public throughout the office. She’s very upset. And I’m thinking, you can’t do this. You know, like I had problems too, but. You’re not going to go into work again. And erm you can see now she’s, he said oh, you know you’re single now. Oh yeah. Do you want to go out for a coffee, and she said, “No, I don’t like you”. Straight off. Good girl. And, and now he’s being iffy with her. But she’s the kind of person who will sit and take it, she won’t tell anybody or anything. But. 

Interviewer:	From a wider perspective, do you think that’s related to the fact that the numbers of women aren’t going in? Or because that women that are in engineering and designing industry maybe a bit too accepting in that environment? 

Subject:	I think we’re too accepting. I do let them get away with a lot. And, some of the stuff though you just expect and you get from the lads at uni like in the vans, when you go out to site, there are copies of FHM and Zoo and everything like that. And at first I thought, “Oh”, you know, not very professional, and you’ve got this van parked on the roadside, and the company logo blazoned all over it. And you walk passed; you get a picture of Jordon, sat there on your dashboard. But, now they’re like, “Oh yeah, phwoar look at her”. I’m like, “Oh, no. No thank you”. Like, “Why what’s up with her?” Like, “Well what’s her personality like?” It’s like “Oh erm I don’t know?” But I think if, something specific to this [town] office, if we had erm because none of the managers here are female. And there’s nobody here in a senior role that is female. (Yeah) And I think that if, for instance, [name] was female or somebody in [name]’s role was female, or a Project Leader such as [name] or [name]. If the guys could see that someone could get that far, then I think they’d treat the other females with a bit more respect. And I think it would balance things out a great deal. But at the same time, there’s a great big deal made about this. There’s a weekly newsletter, if any, any females whatsoever, are nominated to a management position within the UK. There’s a great big spread about it all over the place. Whereas if they are guys, and there’s not. And I can see the point of view they’re trying to, maybe but it could be seen that they trying and encourage females into these roles, and say now these are the possibilities. 

Interviewer:	You can do it sort of thing…

Subject:	Yeah, but at the same time, why don’t they make the big fuss about the men as well? And, I think it’s more of the case of, you know, “Oh my God, look at this”. Rather than a wow, you can to do it to”. Kind of slant on it. But, I definitely. There’s, I think it needs a women’s touch in the office. You know some of the things they do. And some of the presentational skills they use and things, you just sit there and cringe and think, no. You don’t do it like that and, I’m not saying I know anything about business or presenting or anything like that. But some of the communications; the way they tackle situations. You just wouldn’t do that. And if they were slightly more in touch with the members of staff, and maybe a bit more approachable rather than old school engineering than, you know be a lot more at ease overall. Because there is a lot of old school here. (Yeah) And when I first arrived erm when the old engineers, who’s now a very good friend of mine, [name]. He’s used to the drawing board ways and things. And I came in and I was doing the CAD and I’m really settled in doing auto-CAD now. And erm I asked him for some help, and he was like “Oh”. You know you’re student and you’re a girl, why aren’t you making the tea?” And I laughed. And then I realised he wasn’t laughing. And I thought, “Oh God”. And I thought well I’ll make you a cup of tea if you like, and he was like, “Yeah, yeah”. So I made him a cup tea and I deliberately made the worst cup of tea ever. And I’d appreciate it if, if you don’t have time I understand, basically. And, and he replied back saying, “Well you’re the only intern that’s ever emailed me”. And you could have, you know, if he’d replied back and said, “Piss off”. Or not replied back at all. Then that would have been fine, you know because he’s very busy. But when he actually replied back, I thought, blooming heck. You know this is quite good. 

Interviewer:	He must have been impressed with you for daring to email him … 

Subject:	For daring to press send. But I did think I’m not quite sure. I got [name] to read it first as well. But on a professional level, he’s a good manager. Apart from the, he does think he can train everybody and everything can be solved. And I don’t agree with that. I think you can be trained if you want to be trained. (Yeah) And to come into [company] you do have to be, you have to have that drive to really want to learn. And yet again that’s when his lecturer side kicks in. And you have to take the rough with the smooth. And I think a lot of people will go into [company] and expect, you know, I have had the university degree and everything. That’s in the past, I’m now kind of like an adult. But you have to prove yourself all over again. But they don’t expect to, but you do. But I don’t know, he does, he does seem to know everybody, which is impressive. But he seems to be on good terms and he’s sussed people out. So, in my book he’s alright for doing that. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. Is there anyone else that you see as like a role model?

Subject:	Um. [name], who I’ve mentioned earlier as well. Because even in my interview, he was absolutely charming. Really, really nice. And he is a cockney, though he worked in [town] for a long time as well. When I was down here for my interview, everyone was saying “Are you sure you’re not going to be homesick?” “Are you sure you’re not going to be homesick?” I was thinking, oh God I’m going to be really, really homesick. And I was fine before I walked in. And I’m thinking this really is, you know it is quite a long way away from [university] never mind home. And all away from my friends. And I’m thinking oh no, but, you know putting a brave face on things. And he said, “Well you’re northern you’ll be fine won’t you?” And, he walked me back to the train station. And he was asking me about [name] because [name] is [county]. And he was born in [town] and there was common ground there and I’ve been to [town] and seen his gran and everything like. So we were talking about the shops and like the hill on the way to the train station and stuff like that. And he just instantly made me feel welcome. But he’s, he’s says “alright kid” to everybody. No matter your age and your, even your status or anything. And you know and he’s “alright mate”. You know he’s - he’s fine. He’s cool. And he can see if I’m snowed under with work or something. And he just makes you a brew. Or he comes along, he’s say, “Oh you’re trying to make yourself look important with all this paper everywhere.” Like yeah, “half of it’s rubbish”. And he’s like “Yeah I expect it is”. You know and just has a laugh. But apart from that. I mean [name] I admire for the, the fact that she has achieved her position where she is. I think she could do a lot better. She’s very, very intelligent and I think sometimes she dims it down. And I. I know that the same thing in same ways and that I know she has ideas and I know that she knows what she’s doing. But she still quietens down about it. Which annoys me. (Yeah) So I was just like you know you have to really put yourself out there otherwise you get nowhere. Erm apart from that I mean, [name], the lady you met on reception, short dark hair. She’s lovely and [name] notices a lot more than lots of people give her credit for. And she’s my Aunty [name]. And she looks after me because her niece [name]’s one of my friends who works, who’s one of the other admin staff. And she’s nineteen so it’s like a similar age group. But [name] looks after me and checks you’re okay and notices if you come in and you look a bit tired or if you’re visiting the chocolate box a lot. 

Interviewer:	She seemed really friendly? 

Subject:	She’s really, really lovely. And I admire her because she doesn’t let the stress get to her. You know people look around and barking at her, have you got the courier yet? And I have missed the courier. And she’s like, well yes I rang you, but if you’re going to be so long then yeah they’re going to go, deal with it. (Yeah) She just doesn’t seem to let anything get to her. I’m sure it does. But she’s very strong and there’s a lot more to her than I think a lot of the other men really, you know they just see her as the woman who answers the phone. But she types letters and everything. Without her, the office would stop. You know the phone calls wouldn’t get answered. All these people who are so important receiving phone calls wouldn’t get them put through to them. So. (Yeah) She’s nice. She really is really nice. 

Interviewer:	So has your placement tutor visited you?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah. 

Interviewer:	How was that?

Subject:	Twice.

Interviewer:	Twice?

Subject:	Yeah I’m honoured. He -

Interviewer:	Was this -?

Subject:	Unfortunately -

Interviewer:	[name]

Subject:	Yeah. [name]. Unfortunately, he was a head of department but he seems to have been given the placement duty role as a semi retirement kind of role.

Interviewer:	Is he taking over, is it [name] - isn’t he the placement tutor?

Subject:	 [Name] is like the head of placement, so it’s about, but now it’s more of a partnership. But it seems that they’ve slightly downgraded him, you get that sense that they have. But he’s quite, dithery in a way, he’s not. Because I met him when I first started uni and he’s not in touch with things about DT’s as much anymore and he’s obsessed with [company] this, [company] that. And you think, well look you know I’m here, I’m not at [company]. And I don’t think that necessarily, you know advertising a company that are laying off staff and going through a major financial hardship. And everything like that, you know I’m thinking this isn’t, you know it looks like a nice company; it’s a lovely office and everything like that. But they’re not doing that well. Get over it, basically. But he is, he talks about the chaps, the chaps in the office and things like that. So, it’s very hard and I was trying to talk to him about [name]. I knew that he was one of the old school kind of drawing board crew. It was like telling the opposition what was going on. 

Interviewer:	Do the university have a complaints procedure or anything if you were having problems on placement?

Subject:	I don’t think they do. I think they only have one for; within like the DT Handbook, there’s a general grievance policy within you know the - the department itself. Mainly with staff I think. And I know a fair few people have been through that, but that’s when they haven’t been able to hack people being critical about their work. And they do take it more as a, a personal criticism. I mean I’ve had one or two tutors who, well one in particular, [name] who really, really does slate you, he still slates me at the end of second year. You know I know he will do when I get back in the final year. But I know I wouldn’t have developed as much if he hadn’t done. I don’t like him and I don’t think it’s good that he does that. But I’m lucky in the fact that I’ve reacted the way I have. But the general attitude was you’re on placement so, it’s dealt with on placement. You know you’re at work.

Interviewer:	Is that how you felt or do you think they should have been more supportive of you?

Subject:	I think, at the time I felt they should have been more supportive and given me a bit more backup really. Because I felt very much by myself at that time. 

Interviewer:	At least like advice on what you should do in the workplace?

Subject:	Yeah. I found that, like [name] was a lot more defensive really considering she doesn’t know me from adam and, and anything like that, she was like, “Well I’m not having any girl on placement being bullied or anything like this”. You know and it was all, the word ‘girl’ kept (lost words) a lot, and I’m thinking fair enough. You know if she wasn’t a woman, I don’t think I would have got the same response of her. But I don’t know, in a way I knew it had to be dealt with through work because then people would respect me, the managers, people who counted. Not, I’m not bothered about impressing everybody. (Yeah) But people who counted would respect me the way I tackled it rather than running to the teacher, type of thing. But I would have appreciated a bit of backup. And a bit of you know, you - you’re doing the right thing. Rather than me one day just having enough and thinking. It got to the stage where I knew I’d bitten my tongue long enough, and if he’s going to say something again, I was going hit him. And I really, and it got to that stage when I thought I have had enough. But, of course there’s a lot riding on this for me. And I don’t want that on my university record. (Yeah) Or you know, to feel awkward about asking for references or anything like that. Because it’s going to look a bit strange if you’ve had a year out and then you know you say, well yes I had a year out, it’s there on your CV but there’s no references, you know, nobody you can email anything. So it will look very, very peculiar. So, I became a bit selfish in a way. I had to start thinking about me and how it would look on me. (Yeah) Oh I would loved to have thumped him. And to be honest I probably still would. As long as if he comes back with his stupid, really, really stupid stuff and you just think, you know have you actually even considered how that sounds? And you get so het up about the smallest of things. And about people not signing stuff. And it’s not, you know he’s not an engineer. He’s an assistant technician. It’s not his role at all to be criticising engineers. And I recognise that I know where the boundary is. But he just doesn’t. And he goes up to [name] and f’s and blinds at him. And he gets away with it. So, he’s lucky in a way because a lot of people would have stopped him in his tracks a long time ago. But at the same time I don’t think they did him any favours by letting him get a way with it. But, well that’s just him, as they all say. But I don’t know. It’s.

Interviewer:	When your placement student came, did they speak to [name]?

Subject:	Yep. And who was [name] as well. And they, openly talked about the issues with [name]. And it was a case, and is it all solved? Yes. Good. That was it. And then I stood there thinking, but there’s so much more to it than this. And I said well –

Interviewer:	Was you in on it?

Subject:	Yeah u-hu. Erm you know I said well actually I contacted HR. And [placement tutor] seemed quite disapproving by that I done that. And I’m thinking well nothing was get - I tried the - the in-house rule first and it wasn’t working, nothing was going to happen. And that was blatantly obvious. (Yeah) But I tried that three times. Look you know, I’ll use the three strike rule. Tried that three times. And then it wasn’t running and crying every time. It was just if it had really hurt me or really got to me. Then, you know I shouldn’t be leaving work in tears. That’s the, the bottom factor basically. But it was a case of, “Oh, did you did - so you contacted HR, oh”. “Well um”. And there wasn’t a well done or er, I understand why. I wasn’t expecting praise for it, but there wasn’t any kind of reassuring act there whatsoever. It was like, oh you know you’re broke the, the old school rule. Basically that’s how I felt. So, I don’t know. It was a bit. I lost a bit of faith in him in a way. Because he didn’t act as I hoped he would have done. But I think some of the other tutors, male tutors at uni would have acted differently, and would have been right behind me. 

Interviewer:	So you would rather have had a different placement tutor?

Subject:	Definitely. 

Interviewer:	Have you been able to be in contact with anyone else at uni?

Subject:	I’ve been in contact with [name] who’s my, who was my first year mechanics tutor, but I started DT three weeks late because of the A level mis-marking. So, [name] really helped me integrate into the course and gave me lots of work, but also gave me work for the future, which the other students hadn’t been presented with yet. So that it appeared that it was smarter than I was basically. So I was more prepared for it. Which got me friends. Not friends to last admittedly but it got me friends at the time, which was what I needed. And you know, he’s like Uncle [name] you know, he is the one, to me like way up here in my estimations because he’s written all the texts books I’ve ever learnt DT or physics out of. And I’d loved to be like him. He’s like the next in line after [name] really. But I email - I emailed him and I said well, you know this is - I emailed him before I emailed [placement tutor], because I knew [placement tutor] would do nothing about it. And I said this is the situation, I think I’m going to contact HR if they same thing happens again. What do you think? Please can you just give me advice off the record, I’m not going to start quoting this if it goes any further. Can you just tell me? And er he’s said er, you know I think you’re doing the right thing, and if it’s got to the stage where you are taking the steps of speaking out against it, then I know you and I know that it must be pretty bad. So do what you have to do. And he wasn’t saying it was the right thing to do. But still having someone there say, yeah that’s okay, was good. But that could have done to have really been my placement tutor. (Yeah) But it wasn’t. So er I don’t think, I think he’s lost enthusiasm with the entire placement thing and it’s more of a visiting places job rather than a, actually seeing the students and being concerned about their development. I think if it was er being ageist now, if it was er a younger member of staff, they would have more drive about it. 

Interviewer:	So he’s just got the travelling round the country job, basically. 

Subject:	Yeah. Yeah. Huh. 

Interviewer:	Erm I think I’ve asked you most things now. Last thing is some questions I asked you last time. It’s not a test to see if you get the same answers but just to see if you’re view has changed since having more experience. So what five words would you now use to describe engineering or, design technology? 

Subject:	It will be very different. Design and technolog, industry or engineering. Well I suppose I’ll have to say engineering industry because that’s what I worked in this year. Erm sexist, emotionless, very, but I think that’s the nature of the (lost words) to be honest. Erm very, very competitive, scarily competitive and I can imagine some people being driven to depression, it’s so competitive. (Yeah) And I don’t think many people have true friends within engineering. And I don’t think any of them socialise because it is so competitive. They don’t want to let their guard down. (Yeah) And that concerns me slightly. I don’t think that’s natural. When you work with people and you don’t know about them. Because I know about who’s got kids, who hasn’t – (Yeah) Who’s into rugby, who’s into whatever. And some of them sitting next to them, and you think, you know looked surprised that they’ve got children. So, erm two more. Er, very proper. 

Interviewer:	What do you mean by that?

Subject:	It’s erm very, well stereotypically English. It’s very… 

Interviewer:	Everything’s done by books?

Subject:	Everything’s done by the book. There’s a time and place to say things. You act in a, and this is deliberately said, you act in gentlemanly fashion. And everybody abides to that rule. Erm finally, it’s pretty neutral really. There’s nothing. I mean I know most offices are neutral. But it is pretty. There’s a whole. There’s no definite statements anywhere along the line. You know there’s no. It seems like everyone’s been reluctant to make decisions over certain issues, like office layout and things like that. Who - who has what computers? Nobody wants to bite the bullet and say yes. So in that respect everything’s done the way it was done thirty years ago, apart from bringing in computers which I imagine was a great big shock to a lot of people. Erm because it works and why reinvent the wheel? (Yeah) I think, you’re engineers, for god sake, if you don’t reinvent the wheel, who is? But yeah, they’re the five words. 

Interviewer:	So what advantages and disadvantages would you now say there are to being a woman in a male dominated environment?

Subject:	Advantages. You get to get to inside their heads. You erm, I actually understand a lot of my friends a lot better than I did do before I started placement, through spending time with men in a working environment rather than university environment. I can see what make, not - not saying they’re all the same, but you can see what makes some of them tick and, I know how to phrase things, now that things get done, rather than making it seem like a chore or that I’m nagging. And all these other wonderful feminine words that they keep using against me. Erm personally, I achieve - I feel like I’m achieving more if I’ve achieved a goal within a male dominated industry, than a female dominated industry. (Yeah) Because like at Art at A level I used to do well at that but, I wasn’t beating the lads, I was beating the girls. And that wasn’t any fun, that wasn’t a sense of achievement at the end. But I don’t know if that’s just because of having like that particular line of schooling or what. Disadvantages? You have to be very patient and very; you can’t afford to come into work in a bad mood. And you can’t afford to talk about relationships like they do or friendships or anything like, you can’t comment on people. You know even if, no matter how professional you are even if someone annoys you, you go oh God, you know oh - oh. You can’t do that because, because you’re the minority, they pick up on it. (Yeah) And then you’re being bitchy or, you get, well they don’t say it, but you get the sense that they think that or if you comment on someone having a nice tie. Or something, you know just like a general comment or whatever. Like you would to a girl, you would say your hair looks nice, if you know someone’s had their hair cut and then they notice and they wouldn’t in here. I had my hair cut, all the ladies noticed. Everybody else it’s just like, you know we didn’t notice (lost words).. But at the same time if they did notice then it could be misread. (Yeah) And everyone’s very concerned about it, and you do have to think about what you say, before you say it. And check there is no connotations and (Yeah) that you’re not being overly friendly or competitive or anything like that towards them. You have to be, basically have to watch your back. But, I think the advantages outweigh the disadvantages. 

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you still think that women should be encouraged into the industry? You said you wouldn’t recommend this company necessarily.

Subject:	Yeah. I would encourage a certain type of woman into it. And I’m not saying butch lesbian. And I’m not saying geek or anything else that this engineering stereotypical world has to offer. Erm and I think that, for anybody to go into engineering, you have to have a lot of self-belief anyway. But, I would say that specifically for women going into engineering, you really do have to bite the bullet at the end of the day. You have to be able to laugh at yourself. And really take the piss out of yourself. And accept the fact that you may not be accepted, and be okay with that. Because at the end of the day I will always be girl here. I’ll never be one of the lads. I’ll never be a mate, you know, it will be, I will be the girl, the student girl. I think at work, I’ll probably always be one of the girls, type of thing. But you either accept it or you get a chip on your shoulder and bring more trouble onto yourself. So I’d say if you’re determined and strong then do it, and you’ll go far. But if you have a tendency to; I mean I’ve toughened up a lot since I started uni. But if you don’t have like the initial kind of ingredients towards it. I mean it’s all very good being able to do the grades, being able to do the sums. But it’s hard to do that when you’ve got people; you could be perceived as people getting at you around you. So. 

Interviewer:	You said that [name] acts very differently to you, so do you think that she’ll carry on in the industry? 

Subject:	No. I really don’t because the differences between [name]; I’ve got my own project now. I’m in charge of ASR Management, which is archive silicon reaction. Which is, it’s deadly, Bridges but I’m really passionate about, because that’s, that’s my thing. That’s my little baby really and it was originally, handed to one of my colleagues, [name] who’s a really good mate. And now he’s been assigned on to another project so it’s now my thing, really I’m in charge of it, looking after it. And I’m assigning tasks, and sorting out people’s timesheets and it’s fantastic. But I can say no, you book your time over there and I’m getting it under budget and stuff like that. And I enjoy it. But she’s not been set any of those tasks. Because she hasn’t pushed the boundary. She hasn’t actively shown she’d be comfortable with it. Because, you can’t give someone a leadership role if they constantly need reassurance. Which sounds harsh. But it’s true. If you sound unsure of yourself, no one’s going to give you the responsibility.

Interviewer:	No-one’s going to believe anything you say?

Subject:	It’s like if you’re selling a product, if you, if you question yourself, you’ll never be able to sell it, no matter how good it is. You just won’t. And I think she’s going to have to get over that, at some point. And we’ve had discussions about it, and she thinks I’m too, she say’s I’m mouthy. And I don’t think I’m mouth y- I’m opinionated. But I think I’m opinionated at the right times. And I’m not going to hold my tongue when it comes to trying to further myself. But I know the time and place to do that. But, she needs to toughen up, she really, really does. Because she’s going to get trodden on. And I think if I wasn’t here, she’d, I know this is going to sound really big-headed, but I think if I wasn’t here, she’d get treated worse than she already does. Because part of the way in the past, when someone says something to her, and they’ve upset her. It’s come down to me going up to them and saying, “You know, that was a bit harsh and ease off a bit”. (Yeah) But and there you go. That’s me. Xena warrior princess. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. So how would you summarise the placement experience?

Subject:	Erm, eye opening.

Interviewer:	Positive? On the whole?

Subject:	I could be a true engineer and say neutral. Erm.

Interviewer:	Are you glad that you have done it and not just carried on?

Subject:	I’m glad I’ve done the placement. I think if I had of carrying on, I would have had a nervous breakdown. But I’m being perfectly serious, after all the pressure of the work and. I did need some time out. And the fact that this goes towards my course is convenient in that respect. But I think I’ve learnt more about myself than engineering in the placement so far. And the fact that I can tackle things that I never dreamed I can tackle and I can go into a board room with all these big bods, and talk about structures and actually be listened to is amazing, considering when I first came here, I was like “What”. You know, what are you talking about? And there’s so many little details, you know like I’m on the train, I see - I see different types of bridges and stuff and I notice different defects and things, “Oh heck, ooh look at that”. And I think you’re such a geek. Shut up. You know when you like have that voice in your head, and you think “oh dear”. “Oh that’s going to need checking up”. So you think, “Oh no”. And I talk to [name] about it, and [name]. They laugh at me, “Oh you’re so boring, all you talk about is bridges”. So in a way, I’ve kind of taken to it. But it’s not DT. Because DT’s my passion. But, I think it’ll make me a better employee, in the future. (Yeah) And if I ever come across anybody that’s like [name], then I won’t let it go so far. And I’ll just nip it right in the bud and that’ll be done with. I’m not going to get into the, you know quite a few months of build up of resentment and annoyance and upset. It’s just not going to get that far, it’s not worth it. So, I’ve learnt, I’ve learnt lots of lessons that I don’t think I’ve realised yet. When I get properly into work or back to uni, then I think I’m suddenly going to realise how different things are. I think I’ve got used to it now and everything’s normal.

Interviewer:	Do you think it will be strange going back to uni then? Do you think it’ll, it’ll take time adjusting again?

Subject:	Definitely take time to adjust, yeah. I think I’ll probably talk to my lecturers more as equals than as kind of teacher figures. Because I’ve dealt with the people here who are like similar kind of levels of se - seniority. But I think that’s what final years all about anyway. You know you start calling them by their first name apparently, so I’ve heard. But I think I’ll be a lot more chilled out in the final year. Because it will be my own deadlines that I’ve set myself. And obviously its work deadlines but smaller deadlines. 

Interviewer:	Will you use anything that you’ve done here for your final project? Or will that be more design?

Subject:	I may continue with my dissertation and look at it more from the ergonomic and mechanical aspects of this product I’m going to design, which I haven’t got a clue what it is, not yet. But everyone seems to think I have, but it’s just like a blob of plasticine in my mind. And I’m just trying to, you know leave it to form itself. So it’s a back up plan. It’s a very comfortable back up plan. But you know of course I want to re-design the wheel, and come up with something that nobody else has ever done and make it work. But that’s me, that’s what I’m like. If someone says I can’t do something, then I’ll put every single drop of blood into trying to do it. But I’m just stubborn as hell. Anyway I don’t think that is a girl trait or a boy trait. That’s just you know, who I am. (Yeah) But. You know. 

Interviewer:	Ok, that’s everything. Thank you very much for your help.

turns.text: Do you think that more girls do the BA?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely. Definitely. Definitely because I mean not many do the BSc full stop. There’s about twenty in the mechanics class and the materials.
