(Yeah, that’s true) But it’s not too bad. But I’m used to that. I’m used to having more lads around than girls. And it seems strange if there’s more girls around. (Yeah) It’s okay but I’m quite outgoing, so. If I feel that anyone’s feeling awkward around me, or whatever, I’m more likely to talk about it and say, “Right you know, what’s your problem?” Rather than worrying about it and go all quite and shy. Which I thinks put a few of them. Well, shaken them up a bit and, but now they’ve accepted me. But, it’s hard going out here because there was lots of site works and I’ve been involved, [name] who you met, is the Head of the Northern Ireland team which I’ve been put into. And that’s now just finishing off, so, wherever they’re doing nights in Belfast. (Right) With armed police going passed in case of IRA bombings. And, going up and down really slope, steep embankments at the side of the bridges. And gale force winds and snow. And everything like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How long were you there for then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ve been out there eight times now, just for a week each time. So you stay in hotels over there with the drillers and whoever’s sub-contracted. And the engineers as well. And the first time it was very strange. It’s like being on holiday but not. (Yeah) With the really strong accents and everything, it’s you really clear you don’t fit in. But then, after that, still I think a lot of the guys, you know, they’re saying, “Are you okay doing this?” And I thought, well if he can do it, I can do, there’s no problem there. So it’s like, “Are you sure you’re okay?” And it’s just; it’s alright because there’s a tiny bit of sexism in there. And some of the things where they just don’t think. It’s like guys like, toilet facilities, wonderful, where erm you know obviously it’s easier for them just to jump into the back of the field at four o’clock in the morning. Whereas I’m like, erm no. You know I can’t do that. Yeah, and I’m still learning to drive, I’ve got my test at the end of March. So I’ve been learning whilst I’ve been down here and it’s a case of then me having to say so well look, you know, please can you direct me to the next service station? Because they’re all on the motorways anyway, on the bridges. And I’ll, oh you girl aargh. Well but, it depends. Like normally, it won’t bother me but four o’clock in the morning, you’re down there, shout, “Go away”.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do they have porta-cabins or anything?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not at all. It’s take as little as you need over there basically. But, apart from that ...

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have to wear safety clothing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: U-hum.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Clothing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that fit you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We’ve got all the PP. It’s like the standard Health and Safety stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But is that all men’s sizes?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. And er you go through issues with the guys trying to kit you out. And because all the safety boots are in men sizes as well. So, I had to get a size five and I’m a size seven. And stuff like that but also the, the big yellow coats. Obviously, chest sizes appropriately. So, I now have, I’ve got massive a coat, but it fastens and its comfortable, you can move around and stuff. But, that doesn’t bother me. That side of me doesn’t really; I’m not too fussed about it, because it’s the same through DT, so I’m used to it now.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But is it right?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s not right, no. But you know like everything fastens on the male side and everything. But when you’re out on site, and of course, there’s no make up, hair tired back. The hat pulled down, you know. And some of the guys go, “Oh God, you look different”. And I’m thinking erm, “thanks”, they wouldn’t say that if it was another bloke. And about, “Oh look at you all (inaudible) in your site jeans and everything”. “You look different”. I’m thinking well, I’m not going to wear this to work. And I’m not going to wear a suit on site, so. (Yeah. Well you wouldn’t…) Exactly. There are a couple of the comments where you just think, hmmm.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What proportion of your work is out on site then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Quite, quite a lot. It was initially. Now it’s about forty percent. But there’s [name] here as well, who’s one of the engineers, and she’s a tomboy. But she’s really, really nice. And she’s paved the way a lot and I was out on site with her, down in Cornwall for the first few times. And she basically toughened me up a bit and sort of sliding down erm slippery slopes and towards rivers. And you’re sliding down sloped towards motorways and stuff. And you get lorries beeping you when you’re out there. Because you’re a girl and you’ve got bunches or whatever. And erm at first I was a bit like, you know, what on earth is going on? Yeah. It’s just like, come on, you can’t do this when the lads are there. You’ve got to, you’ve got to toughen up. You’ve got to just take it on the chin, or else you’re not going to get anywhere. And if it wasn’t for her doing that then, I think things would be a lot different now. But, you get used to it now, you just laugh it off and if lorry drivers beep at you, and you, and you just like do the honking the horn back at them and. Just take it on the chin, because you’re going to get it wherever. I’m a lot more laid back about it now. It used to really annoy me. And in DT it used to annoy me. But now, when I first arrived, I was thinking “God, it’s followed through to the workplace now”. It’s the same, old boy, you know kind of logic to a lot of it. And [name]’s very heavily involved in the [name] Club. He’s the chairman. And I was invited along twice now. And I was the only woman in the room. And they were like accountants, engineers, doctors, policeman and everything. And they were all, you know, this is the placement student for engineering. And er one of them actually said, “But you’re a girl”. And I went, “Well spotted”. But, I don’t know. In a way, I’m. I used to see it as a bit of a disadvantage. But now I’m turning around as I am different, and I can communicate better than a bloke or most of them here anyway. And I’m confident. But at the same time, I can reach both males and females. I don’t have to, you know, try and tone down the language for anyone or anything like that, I’d just be straight me. And I’m fine. So, I’m seeing that more as a plus point than a downside. So, things are changing, definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, I’ll go through some of my questions then. Do you want to tell me a bit about [company] or do you want leave that for [name] to do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You can have my interpretation of [company].

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Then I can compare them.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: U-huh. [company] is a big American owned company. Head office is New York. (Right) So we don’t very often hear from New York to be honest. Erm when I first started here, I got the impression it was a smaller company. And I was amazed to found out, there were offices throughout all of the world basically. Europe, Asia etcetera, etcetera. Erm this particular [town] branch, upstairs is to do with structural engineering, civil engineering. Downstairs is to do with highways, traffic management, traffic counting. Highly exciting stuff. Upstairs is split into to SIG, which is the Structures Investigation Group, which I’m part of. Led by [name], [name] and [name] and then there’s the bridge designers. And then there are people who look at really severe problems in our little group.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Where are there other bases in the UK then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There are. There the head offices are in [town]. They keep calling it. Erm [town], [town]. Then the main one[town] as well. But there are lots of little sub-offices scattered throughout. And there are about four down this neck of the woods, [town] and [town] and here. (Oh) But, a lot of the offices are quite a stand alone. They don’t work so much with the other offices. But er it fiercely competitive. And everything is.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Competitive, within the organisation or what the organisation do is competitive?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Both. Everybody’s on promotional run. And it’s a kind of atmosphere where anyone will work any overtime whatsoever to get a few brownie points. And I’m not in that frame of mind whatsoever so, but as far as I’d see, I’m placement student. I can’t be promoted. (Yeah) If I was, it would cause major tax issues. So, I don’t know. But there is a lot of stress and pressure about promotion and there’s a lot of erm bickering about the status and things like that. Going on, that I’m aware of round and about. But it’s quite; it’s a challenging atmosphere really. Because some of the things; you’ve got to; everything’s somebody says, you’ve got to take out the situation and think, right what do I know about this company or this person? And what they’re saying, are they likely to have said this? Or done that? Because everyone puts this slight slant on it to benefit themselves. Which I know is the business world and everything but.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has that taken some getting used to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um definitely. Because I’m used to just like at university, people saying like this is good, this is bad. You know, this is what this company does. You know and they give you a fair and unbiased, supposedly un-biased opinion. Whereas here, [company] are always the best. And, and it is good but there’s a lot of emphasis on training and the personal development, which is good. And a large IT support network, and everything like that. So there’s always somebody you can turn to. And erm like the HR Department and Public Relations to do with bullying and everything like that, which I have had experience of here. And it’s just; there are certain levels where there are all these supposed facilities that, you know people you can talk to, people who help you etcetera, etcetera. But there are limits and, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: By that, do you mean that there are polices in place but in reality …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It reality it doesn’t happen. (Yeah) Because there’s this entire three strike rule. The situation I was in, I may as well tell you, the guy whose in the kitchen, the blonde guy, [name] erm had issues with me about being a student. And erm the situation is [name] and I are writing our dissertations, basically regarding the development of equipment for site. There’s lots of time being wasted and the products are just like bricks and it’s awful. And ergonomically, I can’t hold it because it’s too deep for me. You have to hold it like that, but it’s so uncomfortable, whereas the guys you know, they’re all, alright. But yet again, it’s this, not catering for women whatsoever and everyone was saying, “Oh this is dreadful”. “And I wouldn’t design this”. But, you know, it was like, “Oh well, that’s engineering for you”, shrug of the shoulders. Erm but [name]’s taken a great dislike to the fact that, I’m saying things to [name], because I’ve learnt there’s a certain way to tackle things with [name]. And there’s certain steps you go through to get listened to. And you really do everything properly. Erm keep all your emails and remind him of stuff tactfully. I’ve learnt a lot of about diplomacy. Like that, and all the proper introducing people and keeping records of telephone calls, everything like that [name] really, really likes, he’s a very organised gentleman. So I’m in [name]’s good basically and [name]’s took a great disliked to me for that. And started calling me things like fucking bitch, in the workplace and erm the guys shrugged it off, because that’s what [name] is like. So I told [name]. [Name] is of the frame of mind that you can train anybody to do anything. And of course it looks bad on him if one of his members of staff are doing that, erm and this carried on for, this was about a couple of months ago. And this carried on for a couple of months. I thought, right this clearly, nothings happening. I told [name], I told [name] as well. [Name] sat and witness it. Didn’t to anything. And erm and [name] said well if you were a bloke, you’d just shrug your shoulders. And I’m like, “well, I’m not.” And this isn’t professional. I don’t care if they’re male or female, this isn’t professional in the workplace and I’m not being targeted because I’m female or because I’m a student or because I’m at university. Or anything like that, it’s just not on. And I think that took them all back a bit. Because then this initially quiet placement student has had enough. And I thought right, you know, I’m putting my foot down. And so I rang up [name] who’s one of the big bod’s in HR in [town] and she wasn’t having any of it. She was all for coming down here and meeting them and sorting them out and. Which is an amazing response compared to, what I’d had, just you know, keep a log of it. Which doesn’t do anything, and of course I get more tense and more sensitive as to everything he’s saying and doing. And it feels like everything he says is an attack on me, type of thing. And I was trying really hard not to, you know be like a typical prima-donna, and burst in tears or anything. But at the same time, I thought I’m not going to take it. I’m not willing to take it. And when [name], and when I spoke to [name] and told him I’d been in contact with HR and I had a erm a copy of the Grievance Policy. And I knew what my rights were. And if something wasn’t done, then I was going to follow this through with our without his support. (Yeah) Then [name] got called in. But this is months after, and he does it to everybody, but he’s particular focused on myself, [name] and [name]. And he’s still here.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s a coincidence, that you’re all women.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah exactly. But I mean he’s been here two years now. And it’s on the grapevine. Everyone moans about it and everything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But nothing ever gets done?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No because you know he’s had his three strikes and supposedly out but he’s still here. And now, I actually said to him right outside. I thought if I can’t tackle you the proper way, I’m going to tackle you the male way. Like come outside and we’ll go talk about this. He’s like, “What?” You know like, right come on. And everyone’s like “Oh dear what’s she going to do?” And so, we’re outside, you know off the driveways, so its not company property. I said right, “What’s your problem with me? You’re not in work, no ones listening, what’s your problem with me?” And er he said, “You have greater earning potential than me.”

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So basically, he’s just jealous?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Er well let’s go to uni then. It’s not my problem. It’s your problem. Deal with it. And walked back in. And he’s been fine with me now. But I shouldn’t have to take it that far. I mean things now are a lot better between us. Obviously, I’m still a bit a wary as to what’s going on and, if he really is genuine or if he’s still slagging me off or anything? But I don’t expect to be friends with everybody.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did the other two girls react to that then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [Name], [name] just laughed it off, because [name]’s thirty. So she just use now. She goes home at the end of the day and that’s just work and whatever. And he’s just sad. [name], I think if affects [name] a lot more because [name]’s very quiet. And not being racist but I think that’s a cultural thing as well. You know she’s, she speaks when she’s spoken to. (Oh) And she greatly respects men and. (Yeah) A lot of the time, she’ll side on a man’s side even though, he can be blatantly wrong. And she doesn’t offer her own views or opinions. I mean to me, she says, rah rah rah, all these views and opinions and everything. But then, put her in a situation where there’s anybody on any level, and who’s male and she just won’t say it. So I think I’m now seen as the outspoken one. But, I’m not really. I used to be a lot more outspoken. I’m having to turn it down and keeping thinking well -

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think what you have done has stopped him acting like that towards the other people or is he just better with you now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: He’s just better with me now, he’s still the same with the others. (Yeah, yeah) But I basically; I told him straight. I said, “Well look I’ve been in contact with [name] who’s”, you know mentioned the name. And she’s quite fierce apparently, although I’ve never met her but apparently she’s quite fierce and very to the point. And erm I think then he realised I was taking it seriously.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s quite brave of you.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I just got.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Actually doing something about it.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It got to the point though where; I mean I know [name] down here. I’ve made some friends through work but they’re work friends, they’re not friends.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Work colleagues?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Exactly. And most of my friends are on placement this year. So I didn’t want to go back to university. It’s too late to do my final year anyway by then. And it got to the stage where I wasn’t looking forward to coming into work everyday. Not that many people do anyway. But, I really dreaded it. And when I was having my driving lessons, and I was having them straight after work, my driving instructor said, “Oh has [name] said something today then”, because, I was really tense and I was thinking at the end of the day, it came down to it, I felt I’m wasting money. Paying nineteen pound an hour for these driving lessons, if its going to take me half an hour for my driving instructor to keep pulling me over and telling me to calm down. And you’re thinking well, I’d just had enough. And it was the case of me moving, me quitting and going, or it being sorted.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you tell the university what was going on?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ve told my placement tutor, [name].

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And was he supportive?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm he’s very old school. He’s like [name]’s era. And he’s said, “Oh I think you’re probably being a bit hypersensitive” And this is all through emails. I was being very discrete about it and everything and erm because I said, you know, “He’s made some very offensive comments”. So I actually typed down to him everything that [name] said to me. So I have logged it down, it’s in my log book. Then he says, “Keep up a log book you know for you’re placement year, and I thought, right, you know, so I typed it all down. I said there are these ten cases, and I this is what he’s called me. And it’s all kinds of language and it’s all, a lot of it is female specific. And I says er, “Would you put up with that?” You know, because he’s got daughters. And I says, “If you daughter experience that at work, how would you feel?” And then, he became a lot more supportive. But beforehand, it was, “Er well you know some of the lads get abuse, and just take it because you’re a student”. But I’m not this year; I’m a member of this organisation. Which Donald sees and recognises but I think some of them do still see me as just a student, you know. But it’s interesting, but the first thing that [name] said on the phone was, “Would you like to transfer to Manchester?” “Because, because I’m from Preston so then I’d be closer to home, is it just that you’re homesick?” And I said, “No, because I’m staying here. If I can I’m staying here and I’m doing my time here because I’ve started here and I’m not a quitter. I’m not going to move. I’m not causing the problem”. And I’m not. You know so, I said if you want to move someone move him.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So even she was a little bit ...

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: And then when she saw I was digging my heels in, and she did the entire well you know, you may have to make the example of him and then, are you really willing to take the repercussions of this? I’m thinking well, but someone’s got to. Because, I’m going to be in a position, in a couple of weeks time where [placement tutor] emails me and says, “Do you feel this placement would be suitable for another student?” And [name]’s very keen for er the next student to be a girl as well, to keep the mix in the office, you know. And I was thinking I’m going to say no, at this stage, because I’m not going to put somebody else through this. (Yeah) And, you know, it goes through a phase of you know, you get chatted up initially, and then you’re mates and then you get the abuse . And it’s just not on, basically. But, I’m lucky in the fact that I’ve got a long term boyfriend. So, they’ve met each other. And he’s been backed off in that way as well. Whereas [name] isn’t in the same position. So she’s still a target. But, that’s up to her to do something. (Yeah) This year I’m, I used to take a lot on myself. I used to try to protect everybody within my social circle. And this year, it’s a case of right well, its dog eat dog, you look out for yourself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Everyone for themselves?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: And yet she doesn’t want do it. And I’m thinking, I can take it so far and say this, you know [name]’s well aware of what she’s experiencing, because I’ve told him. Erm but if she’s not willing to do anything about it, there’s nothing more I can do about it. (Yeah) So it’s not my problem. Which sounds harsh and my opinion would be the same if she was male or female. Because everyone else has to deal with it, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you meet the student who was here before?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [Name], yes I did. Erm very loud, a bit of Casanova. Erm he, he seemed to get a long with everybody. He seemed like ideal as well really. But he did warn me about [name]. And he said not everybody erm, not the f - the face er, lots of people show you isn’t necessarily as they say, their true face, especially in the case of [name], so watch your back. And, at that time [name] was being absolutely charming with me. So I thought, what are you on about? You know, but, I was warned. But he’s younger, [name]’s younger sister’s here this year. Erm because she started at Loughborough but they put her down erm, what’s it called? Down near [name]. They put her in a mature student block, so she was the only fresher. (Oh no) Exactly. So, she didn’t get out in the fresher’s week and she didn’t enjoy it or anything. Because she doesn’t get to see, you know go into the uni or anything. You’re not going to go by yourself and things like that. So erm she left, so she’s down here for a year. And you can see it all over again, [name]’s trying to make a move on her. And she’s going to knock him back.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you can physically see happening, what happened to you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: And now she’s say’s, you know his, she dumped her boyfriend, and it’s very public throughout the office. She’s very upset. And I’m thinking, you can’t do this. You know, like I had problems too, but. You’re not going to go into work again. And erm you can see now she’s, he said oh, you know you’re single now. Oh yeah. Do you want to go out for a coffee, and she said, “No, I don’t like you”. Straight off. Good girl. And, and now he’s being iffy with her. But she’s the kind of person who will sit and take it, she won’t tell anybody or anything. But.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: From a wider perspective, do you think that’s related to the fact that the numbers of women aren’t going in? Or because that women that are in engineering and designing industry maybe a bit too accepting in that environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think we’re too accepting. I do let them get away with a lot. And, some of the stuff though you just expect and you get from the lads at uni like in the vans, when you go out to site, there are copies of FHM and Zoo and everything like that. And at first I thought, “Oh”, you know, not very professional, and you’ve got this van parked on the roadside, and the company logo blazoned all over it. And you walk passed; you get a picture of Jordon, sat there on your dashboard. But, now they’re like, “Oh yeah, phwoar look at her”. I’m like, “Oh, no. No thank you”. Like, “Why what’s up with her?” Like, “Well what’s her personality like?” It’s like “Oh erm I don’t know?” But I think if, something specific to this [town] office, if we had erm because none of the managers here are female. And there’s nobody here in a senior role that is female. (Yeah) And I think that if, for instance, [name] was female or somebody in [name]’s role was female, or a Project Leader such as [name] or [name]. If the guys could see that someone could get that far, then I think they’d treat the other females with a bit more respect. And I think it would balance things out a great deal. But at the same time, there’s a great big deal made about this. There’s a weekly newsletter, if any, any females whatsoever, are nominated to a management position within the UK. There’s a great big spread about it all over the place. Whereas if they are guys, and there’s not. And I can see the point of view they’re trying to, maybe but it could be seen that they trying and encourage females into these roles, and say now these are the possibilities.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You can do it sort of thing…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, but at the same time, why don’t they make the big fuss about the men as well? And, I think it’s more of the case of, you know, “Oh my God, look at this”. Rather than a wow, you can to do it to”. Kind of slant on it. But, I definitely. There’s, I think it needs a women’s touch in the office. You know some of the things they do. And some of the presentational skills they use and things, you just sit there and cringe and think, no. You don’t do it like that and, I’m not saying I know anything about business or presenting or anything like that. But some of the communications; the way they tackle situations. You just wouldn’t do that. And if they were slightly more in touch with the members of staff, and maybe a bit more approachable rather than old school engineering than, you know be a lot more at ease overall. Because there is a lot of old school here. (Yeah) And when I first arrived erm when the old engineers, who’s now a very good friend of mine, [name]. He’s used to the drawing board ways and things. And I came in and I was doing the CAD and I’m really settled in doing auto-CAD now. And erm I asked him for some help, and he was like “Oh”. You know you’re student and you’re a girl, why aren’t you making the tea?” And I laughed. And then I realised he wasn’t laughing. And I thought, “Oh God”. And I thought well I’ll make you a cup of tea if you like, and he was like, “Yeah, yeah”. So I made him a cup tea and I deliberately made the worst cup of tea ever. And the tea bag hardly touched the water. And er he never asked me to make him a cup of tea again. (Good tactics) You know, I mean there are some managers who erm this guy called [name], who is lovely and he’s got daughters as well, which is a direct denominator I’ve found with a lot of them, if they’ve got daughters, they treat you differently. (Yeah) And if I’m making, because he’s in a little office by himself, but if I’m making a brew, then he’ll offer to make you one. Because he’s left out of the group. And he does the same, and everyone’s like, “You’ve got the manager making you cups of coffee”. And he’s, because it’s good, but doesn’t see, I don’t think he sees it like that. He sees it more as, someone who works in the opposite office, opposite to him, is helping him out. (Yeah) Rather than me being a girl, he sees passed that. But now [name] has to come and help me with helping him with CAD and everything. He’s like, you know it’s just because you’re a girl and you do things thoroughly. So, the slant has changed completely there. But it’s quite good though. He’s like, “I still remember that cup of tea you made for me”. And I’m thinking, well, I’ll never live that one down.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. The day that you leave, you can tell him you did it deliberately.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh I learnt that doing placement at GCSE. When I erm went to the surveyors and ended up making tea all week. And by the end of the week I was deliberately making the most awful tea ever. Just so I didn’t have to do it again. But, there you go. We’ew meant to be good at that though aren’t we, kitchen skills. (Oh yeah) So I keep being told. And I’m like well I can’t cook properly and. And I’m quite open about it. And, like the other week I was off one day because I didn’t properly cook through some chicken. And I say, “Well you know, women are supposed to be”. You know so good at cooking, you know, and here I am giving myself food poisoning, you know. And just laughed it off. And I thought, I’m going to do it rather than let them do it before for me. And it worked and it was fine. But, now some of them though. You can hear some of the guys talking about some of the women who work here. And it’s a case if she’s alright? And you know if they’re not talking about her, she’s got a good personality or ...

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: She’s just good at her job...

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah or anything like that but, you know as soon as. If a bloke’s stressed out, and this is one thing that really, really irritates me. If a blokes stressed out, they’re just having a tough day, and we’ll talk to him tomorrow mate. But if a women’s stressed out or you know, slightly rushed or anything, oh it’s PMT. And er at first I kept quite but the other week, [name]’s like, “Oh, oh PMT”. Like you know “next week it will be. So don’t you dare say it then, because you’re really be in trouble”. And he just laughed it off you see, and he hasn’t said it again. But, if everyone else just sits there and takes it, then it just going to be accepted isn’t it. It’s just going to carry on. And then one day when somebody does flip about it, then it’s going to be a dreadful shock and why have they taken it for so long. (Yeah) But, that’s just life isn’t it. It’s quite funny, because even though I’ve been doing this research, I’ve never really experienced being in a male dominated environment myself. Last [date], I had the privilege of going to a conference in [country] about engineering education like ninety percent of the people were men over about fifty. So I was like the youngest there and one of the only girls as well. And I went with my older boss [name]. And at one of the evening things, the guy who was head of the organisation that arranged the conference, told us that he thought we were lesbians. And we were like, why do you think that?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Because you were women involved in engineering.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: “Well you just seem really close”. It’s like he’d never ever say that about two men would he? I was like, [name]’s just looking after me because it’s my first international conference. He was like, “Oh well I don’t mind looking after you”. And his wife was at the conference too. I was like, “Yes, that’s why [name]’s looking after me”. And. It happens though doesn’t it?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But it’s, it’s one thing them even thinking it but to actually say it…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: That’s why I think that, here the higher the position the men are, the more outspoken they are. I mean, any time [name] comes into a room and goes “Oh, do we need a chaperone?” And it’s a bit like, the thing is though; I mean I’ve made a point of, at fifty percent of the work do’s, which there are a fair amount, erm [name], my boyfriend has been there as well, because he’s on placement as well this year in London. And just to keep him involved and just so they know he’s there, and because [name]’s very, very concerned about if you’re home sick and if you getting involved with, and try showing him that you’re not. I’m okay, I’ve this six foot four bloke yeah and I’m fine. But also, I think it’s helped some of the lads accept me a bit more, because I’m not this girl in engineering, I’m this girl. In a way, because I’m with [name] it makes me acceptable to them. Which, I’m - I’m using their logic to my own advantage, but - and I shouldn’t have to. (Yeah) But at the same time, it makes my life easier because the first when [name] and I arrived down here, “Oh you and [name] are very close friends”. And we’ve been mechanics partners for two years ...

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And we don’t know anybody else.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah exactly. And you don’t know, who to, you know on your first day, you don’t know who talks to who or who’s really friendly and who’s trying suss you out. So, plus we’re in two different teams so we’re comparing experiences. And we have the whole “Oh, you do an engineering type subject”. And they don’t understand what subject I do anyway. And they’re just not really that bothered about it, which is fine, you know I’m not going to talk their heads off about it. But, the implicat; they didn’t say it but the implications were there. And I’m thinking, oh yeah. But [name] didn’t get that. No way. You know he was just one of the lads, came down and he’s instantly accepted. But.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’s been an advantage or a disadvantage having another student here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er disadvantage. I’d say. Because within, this will sound really bitchy. I don’t mean it as it sounds, but within uni, erm I’m mechanics partners with [name], because she’s a girl. And because she gets what I mean, and we’re doing mechanics. And it’s a wonderful way of getting a straight pass. Some of the really sexist lads go, “Oh it’s a bit of oil do you want to put your gloves on”, type of thing. And we’re both of a similar kind of approach to things, where you get your hands dirty, you get it done. Fine, end of story. (Yeah) And we can both do everything else that’s required on the course, but we can also do mechanics. Whereas, here she seems to have changed a bit and I am still very hands on. But [name]’s still asking a lot of questions. And she needs a lot of reassurance. And now, you know as far as I see, I’ve been trained how to do it, made thorough my notes on whatever I’m doing. And I’m still learning every day. But erm I’m not afraid to ask but I don’t pester. But she; I’d rather do something - I mean if it’s really, really important, then obviously I’ll make sure it’s right. But if it’s like a quick task, I’ll quickly check its fine. And then go and do it because it’s going to get checked at the end anyway, because we’re students. So everything we do is going to get checked. But she does ask a lot of questions over and over again, constant, constant reassurance. I mean because part of; our dissertations overlaps slightly. And with me she’s constantly asking questions. I’m like, well look, you know we’ve talked about it and you know what we’re doing. And half of it is her input you know. So, this is your side of the thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’m not doing it for you…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, but she knows the answers. (Yeah) And it’s not because she’s thick or anything. Because she’s really, really intelligent. But she does need a lot of reassurance which the guys really, really pander to. And some of them are like, “Oh you know, she’s so sweet”. Because she’s not, you know this five foot ten person going up to them and saying, “Right this is done. Next job.” But at the same time, they’re like, “Ah can’t you just do it? Can’t you just get on with it?” And it’s like you always have to be right don’t you? You always have to be, you know pristine and everything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It’s such a balancing act isn’t it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um. At first I was being, you know when I very first started, I was just being me. But very polite, very pristine, well mannered me. Because that’s the way when you start any job basically. But then, then I swung over too far when I was trying to fit in with the lads. Because I get on better with lads at uni anyway. Because a lot of the girls have this mega hand up about trying to prove themselves. And I’m competitive, but I’m competitive against anybody, it’s not if they’re male or female. (Yeah) Because I don’t see it like that. Because to me, if you see it like that then, you’re just like the guys. Because they just see it like that. So, you’re just as bad. (Yeah) And, but they don’t see it like that at all. And I have lots of arguments about this. Like they come out with all kinds of sexist comments, like, it’s a lad, you wouldn’t expect them to be on time. I’m thinking, sweeping statement, but you know, I just try and take it as it comes. But then, it’s just hard to explain. Now, I’m kind of more the university me, in a way. Because I, on my desk; on my desk I have a picture of Ben Cohen playing rugby. Which is perfect because then I’ve got the totty, but I’ve also got the rugby interest. And they’re like, “Oh you don’t know anything about rugby”. Go on try me. And I do. You know and I mean its fine, my boyfriend plays rugby, and so I can tell them all about different positions and scores and everything. And they’re like “Oh, okay”. And they’ve all got like Caprice and stuff. And they’ve got the FHM calendars up in the office. And stuff like that which at first I found a bit, not offensive but a bit unprofessional you know. You wouldn’t want to take a client in to see that. But er, but most of the clients are male. So they’re not bothered by it and some of the clients go in there and start commenting on them. (Yeah) And its not negative comments either. But erm it’s strange but now; I mean like with my pink cup. I mean at first I had a blue one, but everyone kept nicking it. So I thought right pink and flowery, just go for it. The most girly cup I can find, and nobody nicks it and nobody uses it or anything because they don’t want to be gay. And they’ve all got this major hang-up about if they look gay or not. Oh, you know it’s really, really daft and really insecure. But, at the minute I’m just being me. And I’m still trying to keep the polite business manner thing going. And I do still do the shacking hands thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I find that really difficult because …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I mean most of the guys here are in serious relationships or married. And I mean like [name] and I have been out on the site together and we’ve seen each other at four o’clock in the morning, stood under the bridge. And he’s seen me really, really hacked off, when I’m trying to do all these ch - different chemical tests and I’m (lost words) approved, which is like the accreditation body, everything like that, and I can do the job. So he just leaves me to it, which is wonderful and I really, really appreciate that. I think, because I know some of the others watch you like hell. But he just says, “Right you know, you reckon you can do it, do it”. And I did, so I’m fine now. But every now and again he makes cheeky comments to me, about [boyfriend] or you know about wearing my big yellow coat if I’m popping out to the bank, something like that. And it’s just; it’s that kind of thing, when you’re not sure if it’s office banter or if he’s trying to show you that he’s your friend. Or if it’s slightly more than that or. You’re not really sure, so you just laugh it off. And really don’t reciprocate whatsoever. (Yeah) Because I don’t want to be seen as encouraging it. But there are lots of. Sometimes you, you hear what people say and you think, “Do you really mean that?” And you can tell that someone of them go absolutely bright red when they say stuff, and it’s like. It’s like “It’s alright, I know what you mean”. But, yes, it’s a lot of patience and you have to be willing for them to get it wrong. And that sounds really patronizing. But they have to be willing for me to get things wrong as well. So I come out with some daft blonde stuff occasionally. And I like, no I don’t mean that. And I know the answer, and yet before you - you just ask the question.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you just speak before you think …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. And I think. No. Don’t answer, and they’re like, “oh - oh – oh”, or “whatever, blonde girl, oh - oh – oh”. And it’s like you know, whatever, but I get that at uni off my female friends as well, so. Um that’s what happens. I think if I’d been on a different course like, as [name] put it like media or something, where you know it’s like, I think it’s about seventy percent girls because it’s a lot higher ratio. And, and then come into this situation, I think I’d be terrified. But after with going through DT and everything, it’s alright. But I’m dying to go back to DT. Not simply because of the change, slight of subject. But also because most lads in DT accept that you can do stuff. Because we’ve been through it. I think I said last time, at the first interview, the first couple of weeks you go through a stage where they’re trying to suss out what you can do. If you can use the machinery or not. And they’re trying to be gentlemanly but they’ve trying not to look like they fancy you. Which is a hard line for them as well. But then now we’re all, you know we’ve all grounded ourselves, we all know exactly what everyone else can do. And it’s just a team. (Yeah) Which sounds a bit idealistic, but it really is. Whereas here, after eight months I’m still on that, you know, can you do this? Can you do that? I mean the other day the printer cartridge went in the photocopier. And I was like, well I can do that, you know it’s like something you had to push it back in. And they had five engineers stood round there going, “Now which one is it?” You know, looking at that. Well look the instructions are on the inside when you open it up.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Men don’t do instructions though.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah and like. You know but it’s, it’s like pictorial instructions. Like well look it’s that one. And it’s all colour coded and everything. I’m like, you just do that. And I just shoved them over, got my hands covered in toner. And I’m like, well there you go it’s done. Washed my hand, end of story. No more about it basically. And they’re saying, “Well obviously we loosened it”. (Obviously) And we were just testing you. And they’re serious. And some of the stuff I laugh off. And even when I know they’re serious, I’m thinking I’m just going to laugh it off because it is daft. But, like at the Christmas dinner er I was fortunate (sarcastic) enough to sit on the table on the big bosses and he says, “so why have you gone into an engineering type subject then?” And he said, “Is you’re dad an engineer?” I’m like “no, there’s no engineering history in my family whatsoever.” And I was like, “there’s no technology or industrial history”. Yes my dad’s a librarian. You know you can’t get much further away from it really. And erm he’s says, “So why did you do it then?” So I was like “because I was good at the subject”. He said, “Oh”. And he seemed to be completely taken aback by the fact that you know, I was good at the subject. (Yeah) So why should I. (Not) Yeah, I’m not saying I am now necessarily. But I think he thought it was bit arrogant or a bit forthright to have said it like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But would he have asked the same question of a male student?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No way.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Because it’s just, that’s what men do, they do engineering.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Exactly. But it’s like the things on site where the guys always bring like a straw for a drink and stuff like that if we’re out on site and it’s. It’s nice in a way, and they’re tease me and it’s like “oh we got you pink straw” and stuff like that. I’m like “oh terrific you know, it tones with my lipstick” or something like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have to work with labourers and stuff when you’re out on the site then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you find there is a difference between the labourers and the office men?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Some of them. Erm we work with a company called [name] engineering. And [name] himself is about the same era as my granddad. And he’s from [area], he’s a very straight talking farmer, basically, he’s a farmer by trade. And on site, they’re all these different boring tests. But one of them you have to do four depths of the concrete to find how much chlorides have gone in. Because then it just fizzes like sodium in water and then like the concrete literally pulls off. It’s really, really scary when you see it, you think, I’ve just driven over this. And you see all these exposed bars and everything. But he’s, the first, because I worked with him out in Northern Ireland. And the first time, I saw him and I, I must admit I had a pre-conception, oh it’s an older, you know about sixty, sixty-five. And he’s a labourer. Which sounds really snotty as well, but you know I was thinking, he’s probably seen me, and thinking “Oh God”. You know. And then I went out on site and er it was it nights, and he said, “Have you ever done nights before?” And I was like “No never”. And but, but I said, “But I’ve been (lost words) for a long time. And er I have to say these shoes are a lot comfier,” you know and so we had a laugh. And he’s like right fair enough. And I so I started talking about my granddad a bit, because I thought, you know I’m going to edge it more and, like it turned out they’re both into George Formby and stuff like that. And he was a bit surprised that I knew about stuff like that. But I was talking to him about stuff on; you know stuff from his era, his past and everything. And hadn’t just gone on at it like, I’m really, you know I’m a rocket scientist. (Yeah) And he said, “Do you know what you’re doing.” I laughed and went, “No not really, but does anyone?” He’s like, “No, we always just make it up”. And then, now he’s looked after me. And so, I went out to do some trials for my dissertation last Thursday, and down to [town]. And he was there, he came over and gave me a big, a great big hug and I’ve now got a nickname as well, [name], because he couldn’t remember name, so he called me [name] for some reason. And er which is alright by me. Everyone’s got nicknames. And it’s a lot nicer than some of the nicknames that some people have. But again, that makes me part of the group. And all the guys have accepted me. And in the office, if people ring me up it’s like “Hiya [name]“, it’s not, “Hi Katie”. But that’s cool you know. And everyone just sticks by it. So, I’m accepted.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When I did the first set of interviews, quite a few students thought that they’d have more issues with labourer type people rather than their actual colleagues. But people, on these set of interviews, but people that I’ve spoken to that have been working in the industry a while have said it’s actually the opposite away round, in that labourers … Because I suppose, maybe to labourers you’re not actually a threat because their boss is always the boss. Whereas you’re in competition more with the people in your office … I don’t know?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I mean [name] you know he’s the head of his own company. And he said to me, you know I don’t care less what your degree is in, and I don’t care if you’re doing a degree. But you’re got yourself down here, you’re got yourself a job and as long as you’re working on, not on the benefits or something, then you’re alright by me. So it was like the older perspective on things. So, he’s says, “You’re not lazy. And you‘re not afraid to ask. So you’re fine”. Like as simple as that. He does include er his three sons. Who are about twenty seven-ish. And at first one of them was like “Oh God, you’re a girl”. And erm the entire “oh brown hair and blue eyes”, that’s unusual. So things like that. And I was like, “Yeah”. And I thought it unusual for professionals to point it out, but there we go. So I just laughed it off. And erm you know you get the entire opinions of what bra cup size do you think Jordan is? And I was like, “I really don’t care.” “Why don’t you ask her?” Oops, yes she won’t talk to you. And stuff like that. But then, that’s just general, what happens. But so, he does employ some of the older men as well. And they “dear”, and god it annoys me. If people dear me, “Yes dear”. “Are you okay dear?” “Are you okay love-y?” And they really do, do that. And now [name]; I work with [name] on site now. Especially when there - there’s certain guys like who do “dear” me a lot of, because he watches and he’s smiling away, because he knows I’m absolutely fuming. But, he - because I was proving myself to him, which I shouldn’t have to. But he does do the same way with everybody and makes everybody prove themselves. And he’s absolutely fine and he’s, he looks out for me. He’s my guardian angel. But within the office, degrees and HNDs, HNCs, B-Eng’s and everything. That is a lot more of an issue. But when you’re out on site, everyone’s out on site, you’ve all got a job to do. You all want to get home. And it’s as simple as that. You know. There’s not the competitiveness. Everyone; you know if someone’s working; because you usually go out in two teams. And so it’s one personnel with (?) or whatever. If someone’s working faster than the other, it’s not a race, it’s a case of once ones finished, they should help the other one out. And nothing said about that‘s, what happens on site is left on site. That’s the general rule. But then in the office, if someone has to help somebody out with something, it’s not forgotten and it is mentioned again and again and again. So, but it’s a lot of; it’s all about pecking order. But that happens more with the men than the women. You know, so we just don’t take part (?), it’s just, whatever get on with it. (Yeah) But with the; some of the older managers like the older school managers are very clearly, you know trying to put their foot down, and trying to stop all this innovation. These young kids don’t know what they’re doing and everything like that. But, that’s not directed at women, that’s just directed at anybody who’s younger than them. (Yeah) But. It’s what is expected in a way.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok I’ve got some questions about your course and that now. (Okay) So, how useful has the course been to the work that you’ve been doing so far? Have you used skills from your course? Or is it just totally different?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Totally different. I’ve used; if it makes sense, I’m using the approaches that I’ve learnt on my course, to work here. Because like, at uni you use er pro-engineer. And solid edge, computer programmes like that, and now we use AutoCad which I hadn’t encountered before properly. But I can think you know this is what I do in Pro-E so, how do I do it in AutoCAD. And from learning how to use Pro-E as well, I’ve learnt that, you know you do have to sit at it for hours and hours and hours and really have a good stab at it. And someone can show you something, and it’s helpful. But at the same time, if I sit there and learn how to do it myself, I remember it. (Yeah) Rather than me having to re-ask somebody. You can get the entire rolling eyeballs kind of here we go again. But, the only drawing I’ve used, like rough defect sketches, which I take the Mickey out of and do nice little trees and stuff in the background and pigeons sat on the ridge and. Which raises a few eyebrows from the older members of staff, but so what. And you know there’s no manufacturing knowledge that’s being used or anything like that. And with my dissertation, I’m actually designing this product like more or less like a PDA, that will record the results. And erm in the meeting I can, came out with all about like the vacuum forming, injection moulding. And about different plastics and different properties and stuff to me which seem really, really obvious. And they’re just like, “What?” And.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Because they don’t care or because they don’t understand?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Don’t understand I think. They seem very intrigued that suddenly. Because I haven’t been asked to discuss it, or anything about it. You know you don’t suddenly start going on about it. (Yeah) Something like that. So I don’t want to sound like I’m shouting my mouth off, or being arrogant or boring them. But, I think quite a few of them were quite shocked that I suddenly knew something about manufacturing. And with mechanics the other day, one of the bridge engineers was saying, “Oh, oh I can’t remember the equations, it was to do about load and stress and the strain and everything.” And I went oh - oh - oh. You know and roll it off to him. And he said, “And what units that in?” You know and I told them. And he’s like, “Yeah” And - and he just looked at me, as if to say, “Oh my God”. You know as if I had learnt it off Who Wants to be Millionaire or something, rather than university and it was a bit of a an eye opening situation for him I think. But of course that has been mentioned again. So. We do some bits and pieces, I think I’m learning more here though on like a business side of things and how to hold meetings and. Which I’m not getting taught at uni.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you could be taught that at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, definitely. I mean some of the stuff …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So to have like a module on business skills?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I don’t think. I think it will be good in an ideal world. I mean, I agree partly with what [name] was saying earlier about it not really being feasible financially and time wise and everything like that. (Yeah) But I don’t think people will take it seriously, to be honest. They’re certain modules which I have which are a bit airy fairy. And you sit there and you think, “And why are you telling me this?” You know what relevance does this have. Because you just have a physics lecture. So you’re very hard it, bashing the hell out of your calculator. And then suddenly you get somebody, you know and I ask like, pretty suit male, you know like pretty suit, very prim and proper or anything. Very well scrubbed. And come in and start flashing away at the power-point telling you about how to act in interviews and things. And you think, you know they don’t know a thing about our subject. And they don’t have a clue what we do. And we, someone asked a question about portfolios and they didn’t even know we had portfolios.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So do you think if it is done, it needs to be integrated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It needs to be done by the. I think it could be done by someone who actually does DT, who’s already built up the respect from the students. Someone like Head of Department or somebody. Or [name], but she’s gone. But that kind of; that was where [name] really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I don’t think there are any female lecturers actually within DT now is there?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There’s [name], who’s the Head of Department’s wife who’s an erg, I can’t say it, but she’s a female ergonomics expert. Erm there are few research students. But that’s it. But [name] is very erm aggressive in her approach. I think she feel she needs to be to, you know get - command the respect off people. And I think she scares the hell out of some of the lads to be quite honest. And they just sit there like. Whereas [name] invited people to challenge her. And then she’d knock them back no problem. But at least, you know you, that’s over and done with. But in [name]’s lectures, she used to do, and you wouldn’t present it like this would you? And what would you do? And she kind of opened things up, so it wasn’t just that lecture till five o’clock and then you go home and what you’re going to have for your tea? turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah I guess that’s what I meant, when I said about integrating the skills.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: But we took it off her because she knows what our subject is. But we’ve had, some of them like, from a careers erm centre. And I’m not saying they don’t know their stuff, they do. And they’re like “is it a bit like engineering?” And you know, “is it more arty?” And they just don’t know and they come in and they just, you know they go “blah, blah, blah, blah”. And we sit there thinking, you haven’t learnt about us, you know you haven’t prepared for us, so why should we listen to you and take any notice of you basically? Which I know it sounds a bit harsh, but I think that’s same with any situation isn’t it? If you haven’t prepared for something then, you’re not going to look professional, and nobody’s really going to take any notice of you. But, I think you only learn, you only really learn about presentations and meetings and stuff when you’re in the real world. And when you do have to sit there through like three hour presentations and they’re all talking about bridges and it goes on and on and on, and they say we’re going to discuss all the structures on the [road], and you think, oh right you know, ok the [road], quite long. I’m thinking not that many structures in fact. So the first bridge, and then you see the first slide is like one out of three hundred, and it’s really warm and you’re sitting thinking, don’t close your eyes. I’m okay. But you’re only going to learn about that when you’re there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So did you have to do lots of presentations and stuff as part of your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And do you think doing that has helped you, like the practical skills, rather than the technical skills and doing group work and stuff like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I think so. But through school as well. Because it was an independent school. So it was like a smaller class and a lot of time was spent concentrating on each of us and our presentation skills and public speaking and everything like that. (Yeah) So that you get the jargon, and you promote school and, you know all very. Again it’s quite old boy type stuff again really isn’t it? But erm.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You went to a girls school didn’t you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. But then it was amalgamated in sixth form, you know. So it’s the same. Basically it’s the same experience of you know like being like at sixth form, suddenly having to amalgamate when I was at uni, and then now again. And I’m getting a bit fed up of having to, in a way readjust again and again and again. And I know it’s a natural life stages but it’s the fact that I’m a girl and the course I’m doing, and my attitudes that are the problems with lots of guys. And yeah I can type. You know I take minutes, that’s fine. But I don’t have to, because I’m the girl. But, I don’t know, I think they; the course has given me the confidence to say what I think because, there’s lots of critiquing on the course. So everyone’s always telling you the truth about your product or whatever and you’ve got to take it on the chin, act professional. Say thank you very much and walk out and mutter under your breath. So, it’s, I find it strange within this environment that people don’t critique what you do, really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s interesting. Although, a lot of the engineering education stuff that I’ve looked at seems to suggest is that in engineering courses, there isn’t really any room for like criticizing and challenging things - you’re just taught and that’s accepted. So maybe you’re course is a bit different in that respect?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I mean I accept I have had to adjust slightly into this engineering world. It is a very strange world. And, like within DT like the BSc modules, there’s obviously a right or a wrong. And like the more BA, the BA side of it, it’s more open to opinions. I’m used to people having opinions in what I do. And because my BSc tutors teach the BA subjects as well, they do say, “Well this is right but you could have done it like this”. (Yeah) Whereas here. It doesn’t happen with me but with a lot of the admin stuff, if somebody does something and it’s wrong, rather than the manager taking it back to them and saying, you know thank you for doing this, but could you just develop it slightly, or make some alterations? They give it to somebody else, to alter it. And that happened to me once and I saw my CAD drawings being pulled up by somebody else and I’m thinking, “What are they doing, those are mine?” So I’m very protective of my CAD drawings. I’m thinking I spent ages doing those. What are you doing? What are you messing around with? And, [name] said “well I didn’t want to offend you”. “Alright, well fair enough, but I’d much, I get more satisfaction out of …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’re not going learn for the future doing it like that.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Exactly. I’d rather do it and learn and say “Oh this bits wrong, this bits rubbish - re-do it”. I can handle that. That isn’t a problem whatsoever. Rather than somebody else having to go into the CAD drawings all different layers and all completely different standards and try and work out what I’ve been doing. So I’ve still got my own little way of doing things. But the. But now that I’ve. It’s the same thing again isn’t it? It’s now that I’ve said that um you know, and they know. People come along and say, “Oh look, you know.” Only the other day, I put May, so in fact the best. Yeah I put May instead of March, on top of the letter and sent it to [name] for approval. He’s says well that’s fine, but I think it may get lost whilst we’re waiting to send it out. And I went, “Um”. I’m thinking, what are you on about, and walked out, and then underneath he made a very discrete pencil line, saying you may want to check the log so I’m thinking “oops”. But then that’s er a one on one thing, there’s no public humiliation going on which is good. Which does happen at uni. And you can tell obviously you know when people are getting, you know told that they’ve done something wrong, and there is lots of “ooh”. But, really; they deal with stuff like that in a professional manner. But apart from that the main thing I’ve used from DT’s mainly when to bite my tongue. Basically, and you know when, you can tell when the lads are getting a bit stressed or when they’re feeling a bit, maybe a bit threatened or you know just generally fed up. And the way that they handle anger, I think is quite different from the way women handle anger. I mean sometimes I get really, really annoyed. But instead of going and hitting a wall or something, I will just discretely slip away and cry. If I get really annoyed I cry, which lots of people sees as a weakness. But it’s not, it’s just I’m so annoyed, and it has to come out one way or the other. But, you know if I’m on site, I was trying to repeatedly do this test area again, and again and it wasn’t working, and I’m really tired, and the rain was literally plummeting down on top of me, because my jackets really big, it was all filling out inside with the rain. Up my sleeve. And it’s really so, oh - oh - oh, and I was getting really annoyed with myself because it wasn’t working. And that’s because I wanted to prove myself, but not as a girl but as me. And prove to yourself . And er like I started crying. And I mean I can’t do this, and I want, and I didn’t going to ask for help or anything like that. But whereas with the guys you can see them when they go quite, and when they start doing the staring motions, and I know from DT lads, that’s when you leave them be. Whereas [name] will carry on asking questions and asking questions and asking questions. I’m thinking oh he’s going to explode in a minute, you know kind of duck . And then they just do; and then they walk away. And she’ll see that as being very, very rude. But I’m thinking, I’d rather be walked away from you, than you experience whatever they’re annoy about it. (Yeah) But, I think that’s different experiences on different friends and.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So how would you say that university and work differ?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Money.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that the main difference?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I love the money, but it’s not. It’s the independence of the money and the fact that. As little as I have to do and even though there’s a wide variety of tasks I do, you know I have to, in fact one of them every day is not really anything new. (Yeah) So, you have your friends who you know, you trust and everything, but apart from that, you - you watch your designs and you watch what you’re doing and check that no-ones, you know, copying calculations and stuff. Whereas here, I feel good in the fact that my works being recognised and I’m getting paid. And that’s, funny that’s quite a good feeling you know. I’ve like got my little place in the world. If I’m late coming in tomorrow, then some of the projects will be held up, which is quite a nice feeling. And I’m a bit of er an awful feeling when you wake up in the morning and think, oh I can’t be bothered. But erm at the same time, I’m not, I - I don’t get the same satisfaction because they’re not my projects. And it’s not my heart and sole that goes into it. You know it’s quite an - an emotionless subject really. There’s n - there’s nothing of me in it. (So…) So if you know what I mean, I’m carrying out tasks.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you feel about working for real, so to speak, are you worried about feeling like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m going to do a Masters and then a Doctorate and everything. I’m going to stay uni, I really, I really don’t want to start work. I think. It’s hard to decide really because this isn’t my niche. This isn’t my thing. And if I was in.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, you wouldn’t -

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not go into engineering? (Yeah) No, no. No way because I mean it’s one thing tackling something for a year. I mean I like the subject. I like the fact that it’s, you know right or wrong and, and you know there are definite rules and regulations. That side appeals to me. But at the same time, it lacks something because you can’t put anything into it. You know there’s no adaptation. We just follow guidelines from, that’s what I see from here anyway. But that may not be all (faculties?)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you glad that you did this placement or would you rather have done another placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm I’m glad I’ve done this one, because I know from my friends that have done others like at [company] and stuff I was shown around there, because I had an interview there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I thought you’d end up there.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: And I thought, you know, you walk round and its really good and I ended up telling turning down [company], at the end of the day. And there was a nice little team and they were all women, which is nothing wrong with that, but there was, you know it was obviously ‘the’ packaging technologist department and everybody else, you know was all mates having a laugh (Yeah) And that was the girl room. And it struck me as a really bitchy environment. When you walked in you could hear them whispering and laughing and giggling and they were just like the stereotypical person in the corner that wasn’t involved. And I’m thinking I don’t want to be in this atmosphere. And I didn’t want it narrowing off my CV. (Yeah) Because within design if you go into packaging. That’s it. (Yeah) You’re in packaging; you know there’s no hope for you basically. But erm the way they sold it initially. When you walk in you think, yeah this is really, really good. And lots of girls go in for it as well. So I was thinking, yeah this could be alright. But then, some of my friends who accepted placements there, because they’ve taken on eight people. And they are drawing out layouts for boxes everyday. And they’re doing photocopying. And sending faxes, and stuff like that. Basically doing admin work. And they haven’t done any design, they haven’t drawn anything at all. So, I mean one of my friends is at [company], who’s supposed to be doing erm -

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’ve interviewed some people at [company]

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well one of them is supposed to be a packing technologist and she’s stirring [product] and testing the viscosity of [product]. Day in day out. And she’s -

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But they do get [product] every week.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: True but she’s being doing it for eight months. You know and she’s my best mate, and she’s rung me, saying “Oh - oh - oh”. You know it’s alright, you get [product]. But it’s alright and I’m thinking well, at the end of the day, I’m getting to interact and even though it’s not specifically my subject. I’m not doing photocopying every day. And I’m being given -

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Not too much and not too little?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: At first it seemed like a lot. When I very first started. Because I was taking over from half way through some of [name]’s projects which he’d been in charge of. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: A special budget, that’s a bit scary …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. And “we’ve always achieved first level KPI’s. So we’re expected to keep this”. And you’re thinking, oh golly, see things like level five which is right at the bottom. And, and sounding sexist again, I used kind of like a shopping logic against things, you know would I buy this if it was this price? And try and reason it out in my own way. But, now that, if you want; even though I can’t get promoted as in like status level, job title, wage. You know I haven’t got to the level where I have my business card yet. But erm I have in a way been promoted because, once you’ve proven yourself, you can do something. I’ve now got a lot more responsibility than I had initially. (Yeah) But I’m just juggling it erm. I’ve learnt now when you say no, when people say “oh, will you just do this,” “no sorry too busy”. And but everyone else does it. And so what’s good for the goose is good for the gander. Because when I walked in there, I didn’t have a clue about the structural engineering or civil engineering or, what the hell they were talking about? turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that even though you don’t want to go into this area, that it will still help you when you eventually get a job?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think; I can see possibilities within [company] because [name], made me feel like I’d always be very welcome.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you want to work for them?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I wouldn’t want to come back here. Because I think they’d always see me as a student. And because they do keep hold of their staff there. (Yeah) And er that kind of thing kind of links in with my course. And like selling the company and how the company’s perceived and brand imaging and stuff like that. That kind of thing appeals to me. But then again, dropping off my B - BSc then. (Yeah) But I would only get that job through having a BSc to get my foot into the company. So I can see me working for other departments of [company], but not specifically this particular branch or this particular niche. But ideally I’d like to work for [company] in the lab. But, you know a bit of way from there at the minute in [town], but you never know. It’s good to have goals. I’m goal orientated at the end of the day. So that’s why I fit in here I think. It’s up to him whatever he wants to do. So.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So what exactly do you have to do to get your DIS?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You have to complete all your logs books, basically a diary of what you’ve done everyday and who’s said what, and mine are quite sarcastic in there. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How many words is that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Five thousand. Which isn’t bad. But I’m seeing it as preparation for my final year dissertation which is nine thousand. And otherwise I wouldn’t have this experience and having you know like, [name] as a lecturer reading through it. (Yeah) Is a bit of er you know it’s a step up, ready for next year. But because [name] didn’t do it erm they basically let [name] and I get on with it, and whatever you want to do, just do. Type of attitude. I think they’re going to be surprised at the end as to how much work we have done. But, I think there will be a certain, like a higher standard for the next placement student, poor person. But at the minute it’s more or less a case of you, is literally you do whatever you have to do. And we’re not going to interfere with it. And they’re interested; you know they want to know we’re doing. But they don’t quite understand why it’s so important that we have this diploma. And [name] and I are furiously trying to explain to them that you know, we’re doing like the DT politics of the eng, you know there are different levels obviously. And if you’re doing a BSc, that’s like one up on the BA. And if, but there are lots of us that are going to get BSc’s. So if you’ve got; you’ve managed to get yourself a placement which is blooming hard. (Yeah) Can you remember like at the last interview, I was stressed about whether or not I was going to get a placement.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Most of your course was

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah I no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Not the students, but the department seem to leave it until after Easter

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s like oh yeah well, you know we’ll sort that out tomorrow. Yeah exactly, and then I spent the whole of Easter thinking, “Oh what am I doing?” But erm I don’t know, it’s just. It’s quite strange in a way because part of me is that DT way. You know well I’ll sort it out later, it’s okay. Erm I’m like that with my log book. Because I’m my own manager on that. But with all my work I always ensure anything I hand into my managers is early. And it’s not necessarily because of the subject, it’s more the environment. And that’s what I was saying to [name], even some women that do engineering don’t go into it at the end of the day. And it is; I’m getting a bit tired of having to prove myself. You know it’s not just proving yourself within the company, but proving yourself because you’re a girl. And proving yourself because you haven’t graduated yet. And everything like that just gets to a point where you think, I can’t be bothered. And I’m me. And you either accept me or you don’t. And, which can course problems.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So does that make you want to go more towards the design side then where there are more women? Or do you think …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In a way yes. But at the same time –

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that numbers do make a difference or not?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Numbers do make a difference definitely. But at the same time, knowing me I wouldn’t be happy if I did. At the same time, it - that’s one of the things that pushes me forward. And it makes me more determined to do better. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s what you’re used to now, is it?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you think that doing team work at uni compares to doing team work at work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s easier at work. It’s a lot easier. And what on earth does she mean?” You know and. You know I’m being the advice giver. But at uni I seem to have been the organiser. And I always seem to be on people’s cases to get stuff done on time. And a bit of a team leader but then when I catch myself being a team leader, when you’re not assigned roles, if I catch myself trying to lead the team, then I’ll try and sit back a bit. But I’m very keen at trying to pull opinions out of quiet people. And try and shut the loud people up. Whereas at work, if your boss, he’s obviously, ‘he’ obviously, he’s obviously the team leader, or she. And erm you know there’s no, there’s no feedback, there’s no tantrums which you get at uni, or people stomping off.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You mentioned being assigned roles, do you think at work it is easier because people already have roles?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Yeah it’s more the fact of. I think it’s because it’s - it’s less personal as well. Because at uni the design side of it, it is your opinions, your heart and sole’s sat down there. In team meetings I do try and push things forward a bit if I think we can achieve more than we’re setting our sights on. (Yeah) But I’m - I get away with that because I’m the rebellious student. But I think if I worked here, like properly full time, then they probably have something to say about it. But at the end of the day, everyone knows who’s top dog. And that’s all it comes down to. At the end of the day, if you want you’re promotion, you listen to your team leader who’s you’re manager. If you don’t, you stay at the bottom and. That isn’t necessarily how it should be. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Even though they’re different, do you think that doing group work at uni helps you when you come to work?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Seems more black and white.
