[Name] erm when I first came down here, my mum came down here as well. You know just for a couple of days to check if I was okay. Because I was offered a job on the Thursday, I was expected to start on the Monday. (Oh my God) So my mum came down erm stayed in a hotel, had to find somewhere to live. Found somewhere to live.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: They, did they put you up in a hotel?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. And erm it’s pretty expensive down here as well. And er.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It’s a bit scary as well being thrown somewhere new.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: And then I moved into my shared house, ten o’clock on Sunday night. Unpacked and started work at half seven on the Monday morning. And I walked in here, and I was, I think the day’s tiredness and confusion carried me through a lot of it to be honest. But, it was very, very stressful trying to find somewhere to live. It was. I knew, I felt a great honour bound not to let them down here. And, I felt that at the same time I could have done with a bit more help. But [name] promised Mum you know we’ll look after her. And we really will type of thing. And they’ve, encouraged me to drive. To learn how to drive and the very amenable with work hours and things, you know when I have my theory test. Erm and I’ve got my practical test at the end of March. Erm I was going, I booked a day off, annual leave and thought, oh no, no, no, you know, you’re going to use your driving skills. You know, you see the big vans in the car park and I’ll end up driving those with the beacons on, which is wicked. And erm yet again quite a male thing. Really big van, oh yeah. And erm.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You can be a white van man?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. And he said you know, it’s the company thing therefore you don’t need to take a day off. So he does look after me. [Name] is my harshest critique. And if I, if I don’t do something that I should have done or, like with my dissertations, you’re constantly in contact with all these different companies. And you have to keep up dating him all the time. Even if he doesn’t read them, he notices if you’ve sent an email to update him. (Yeah) And it’s like on Friday he was off but I rang him on his mobile at lunch time because he asked me to remind him about you coming to see me. And it’s just so he’s always up to date and he knew he was going to be bombarded this morning, after having been off for one day. And he has been, he’s been in meetings all morning. But it’s that kind of. If I do things his way, he looks after me. And I notice that if I start to do stray slightly, then you know things get a bit rocky and he goes a bit quiet with me. But, as far as, at first…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So he’s supportive of you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: If, if I abide his rule, yes. But at first I saw it that my job was to do all the engineering bits. And then for me to keep him up to date via email was an extra bit. You know it wasn’t my task, it wasn’t my work. But now I’ve accepted that it, it does go hand in hand. And that to do well in one, you have to well in the other. But I think that’s work, again basically. But of course he wants to know what we’re up to. But he’s quite good as well. Because he goes out on all the nights out and stuff like I’ve been out playing west country skittles, which is amazing. It’s like, you know like bowling, basically. But in the back end of a shed, in the back end of a freezing pub. And wooden skittles, and it - it’s so awful but it’s good. And you’ve got this like concrete run and a little gas fire at the side, like one of the plug in ones. And then you throw this ball, which does look like a turnip. And it’s basically bowling but it’s skittles. And you have someone at the end who stands up and puts all the skittles back at the end. And you have chalk board and you had to add it up yourself. And I walked in and thought, primitive. Have you not been to Megabowl? What are you doing? But it’s a laugh. And it was really, really good. And [name] then became more of a friend than a, a manager. Because he can do that on social do’s. He is on a level with everybody. At work ...

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s quite good. Where I used to work, other managers came out, but my line manager never ever came on work things. Even like Christmas meal which we went out for during the day. Like in work time, he didn’t come out.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: That’s a bit off really isn’t it? But I mean I think it takes a lot on both sides for [name] to let the side down and, in the fact like his defences down not let the side down and you know be teased along with everybody else. It’s like on site [name] teases him more than anybody else. And you know they’re all friends and the get away with it. (Yeah) But also for us to then treat him as one of the group and act normally around and him is a bit difficult. But he’s okay you know. He’s a. He’s made every effort to make me welcome here. And he was very active in looking around for suitable driving instructors and things like that. So he is looking after me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is he one of the people that’s got daughters? (Yes) It sounds like your his extra adopted daughter…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ve met his daughters, but he’s very, [name] is quite straight talking. And he sees through people trying to, pardon my French, bullshit him. And at first, when I first came here, you know I told him everything he wanted to hear. And he says right, whatever, what do you really think? And he does turn into a lecturer when you’re talking to him every now and again he does say, “Right shut up. You know you don’t know what you’re talking about. You’re going up the wrong route”. And you’re thinking, ah, no. But he’s more, he’s like an uncle, you know and a godfather kind of figure.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel he’s like a role model as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um Yes and no. I admire for his networking skills. Because knows everybody. Seriously. And he’s, he’s written so many articles and anything like that. He’s one of the ones who’s networked through [company]. And made use of the resources through [company]. Which lots of people just don’t see. And they just don’t realise that we’ve got an entire email base full of people. Because I went to the CEO, the Chief Executive Officer, [name] who’s like the biggest boss in New York. And, I emailed him and said this is my dissertation title, if you have any comments or anything you’d like to, you know add that should be taken note in this. And I’d appreciate it if, if you don’t have time I understand, basically. And, and he replied back saying, “Well you’re the only intern that’s ever emailed me”. And you could have, you know, if he’d replied back and said, “Piss off”. Or not replied back at all. Then that would have been fine, you know because he’s very busy. But when he actually replied back, I thought, blooming heck. You know this is quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: He must have been impressed with you for daring to email him …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: For daring to press send. But I did think I’m not quite sure. I got [name] to read it first as well. But on a professional level, he’s a good manager. Apart from the, he does think he can train everybody and everything can be solved. And I don’t agree with that. I think you can be trained if you want to be trained. (Yeah) And to come into [company] you do have to be, you have to have that drive to really want to learn. And yet again that’s when his lecturer side kicks in. And you have to take the rough with the smooth. And I think a lot of people will go into [company] and expect, you know, I have had the university degree and everything. That’s in the past, I’m now kind of like an adult. But you have to prove yourself all over again. But they don’t expect to, but you do. But I don’t know, he does, he does seem to know everybody, which is impressive. But he seems to be on good terms and he’s sussed people out. So, in my book he’s alright for doing that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Is there anyone else that you see as like a role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um. [name], who I’ve mentioned earlier as well. Because even in my interview, he was absolutely charming. Really, really nice. And he is a cockney, though he worked in [town] for a long time as well. When I was down here for my interview, everyone was saying “Are you sure you’re not going to be homesick?” “Are you sure you’re not going to be homesick?” I was thinking, oh God I’m going to be really, really homesick. And I was fine before I walked in. And I’m thinking this really is, you know it is quite a long way away from [university] never mind home. And all away from my friends. And I’m thinking oh no, but, you know putting a brave face on things. And he said, “Well you’re northern you’ll be fine won’t you?” And, he walked me back to the train station. And he was asking me about [name] because [name] is [county]. And he was born in [town] and there was common ground there and I’ve been to [town] and seen his gran and everything like. So we were talking about the shops and like the hill on the way to the train station and stuff like that. And he just instantly made me feel welcome. But he’s, he’s says “alright kid” to everybody. No matter your age and your, even your status or anything. And you know and he’s “alright mate”. You know he’s - he’s fine. He’s cool. And he can see if I’m snowed under with work or something. And he just makes you a brew. Or he comes along, he’s say, “Oh you’re trying to make yourself look important with all this paper everywhere.” Like yeah, “half of it’s rubbish”. And he’s like “Yeah I expect it is”. You know and just has a laugh. But apart from that. I mean [name] I admire for the, the fact that she has achieved her position where she is. I think she could do a lot better. She’s very, very intelligent and I think sometimes she dims it down. And I. I know that the same thing in same ways and that I know she has ideas and I know that she knows what she’s doing. But she still quietens down about it. Which annoys me. (Yeah) So I was just like you know you have to really put yourself out there otherwise you get nowhere. Erm apart from that I mean, [name], the lady you met on reception, short dark hair. She’s lovely and [name] notices a lot more than lots of people give her credit for. And she’s my Aunty [name]. And she looks after me because her niece [name]’s one of my friends who works, who’s one of the other admin staff. And she’s nineteen so it’s like a similar age group. But [name] looks after me and checks you’re okay and notices if you come in and you look a bit tired or if you’re visiting the chocolate box a lot.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: She seemed really friendly?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: She’s really, really lovely. And I admire her because she doesn’t let the stress get to her. You know people look around and barking at her, have you got the courier yet? And I have missed the courier. And she’s like, well yes I rang you, but if you’re going to be so long then yeah they’re going to go, deal with it. (Yeah) She just doesn’t seem to let anything get to her. I’m sure it does. But she’s very strong and there’s a lot more to her than I think a lot of the other men really, you know they just see her as the woman who answers the phone. But she types letters and everything. Without her, the office would stop. You know the phone calls wouldn’t get answered. All these people who are so important receiving phone calls wouldn’t get them put through to them. So. (Yeah) She’s nice. She really is really nice.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So has your placement tutor visited you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How was that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Twice.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Twice?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah I’m honoured. He -

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was this -?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Unfortunately -

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: [name]

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. [name]. Unfortunately, he was a head of department but he seems to have been given the placement duty role as a semi retirement kind of role.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is he taking over, is it [name] - isn’t he the placement tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [Name] is like the head of placement, so it’s about, but now it’s more of a partnership. But it seems that they’ve slightly downgraded him, you get that sense that they have. But he’s quite, dithery in a way, he’s not. Because I met him when I first started uni and he’s not in touch with things about DT’s as much anymore and he’s obsessed with [company] this, [company] that. And you think, well look you know I’m here, I’m not at [company]. And I don’t think that necessarily, you know advertising a company that are laying off staff and going through a major financial hardship. And everything like that, you know I’m thinking this isn’t, you know it looks like a nice company; it’s a lovely office and everything like that. But they’re not doing that well. Get over it, basically. But he is, he talks about the chaps, the chaps in the office and things like that. So, it’s very hard and I was trying to talk to him about [name]. I knew that he was one of the old school kind of drawing board crew. It was like telling the opposition what was going on.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do the university have a complaints procedure or anything if you were having problems on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think they do. I think they only have one for; within like the DT Handbook, there’s a general grievance policy within you know the - the department itself. Mainly with staff I think. And I know a fair few people have been through that, but that’s when they haven’t been able to hack people being critical about their work. And they do take it more as a, a personal criticism. I mean I’ve had one or two tutors who, well one in particular, [name] who really, really does slate you, he still slates me at the end of second year. You know I know he will do when I get back in the final year. But I know I wouldn’t have developed as much if he hadn’t done. I don’t like him and I don’t think it’s good that he does that. But I’m lucky in the fact that I’ve reacted the way I have. But the general attitude was you’re on placement so, it’s dealt with on placement. You know you’re at work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that how you felt or do you think they should have been more supportive of you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think, at the time I felt they should have been more supportive and given me a bit more backup really. Because I felt very much by myself at that time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: At least like advice on what you should do in the workplace?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I found that, like [name] was a lot more defensive really considering she doesn’t know me from adam and, and anything like that, she was like, “Well I’m not having any girl on placement being bullied or anything like this”. You know and it was all, the word ‘girl’ kept (lost words) a lot, and I’m thinking fair enough. You know if she wasn’t a woman, I don’t think I would have got the same response of her. But I don’t know, in a way I knew it had to be dealt with through work because then people would respect me, the managers, people who counted. Not, I’m not bothered about impressing everybody. (Yeah) But people who counted would respect me the way I tackled it rather than running to the teacher, type of thing. But I would have appreciated a bit of backup. And a bit of you know, you - you’re doing the right thing. Rather than me one day just having enough and thinking. It got to the stage where I knew I’d bitten my tongue long enough, and if he’s going to say something again, I was going hit him. And I really, and it got to that stage when I thought I have had enough. But, of course there’s a lot riding on this for me. And I don’t want that on my university record. (Yeah) Or you know, to feel awkward about asking for references or anything like that. Because it’s going to look a bit strange if you’ve had a year out and then you know you say, well yes I had a year out, it’s there on your CV but there’s no references, you know, nobody you can email anything. So it will look very, very peculiar. So, I became a bit selfish in a way. I had to start thinking about me and how it would look on me. (Yeah) Oh I would loved to have thumped him. And to be honest I probably still would. As long as if he comes back with his stupid, really, really stupid stuff and you just think, you know have you actually even considered how that sounds? And you get so het up about the smallest of things. And about people not signing stuff. And it’s not, you know he’s not an engineer. He’s an assistant technician. It’s not his role at all to be criticising engineers. And I recognise that I know where the boundary is. But he just doesn’t. And he goes up to [name] and f’s and blinds at him. And he gets away with it. So, he’s lucky in a way because a lot of people would have stopped him in his tracks a long time ago. But at the same time I don’t think they did him any favours by letting him get a way with it. But, well that’s just him, as they all say. But I don’t know. It’s.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When your placement student came, did they speak to [name]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yep. And who was [name] as well. And they, openly talked about the issues with [name]. And it was a case, and is it all solved? Yes. Good. That was it. And then I stood there thinking, but there’s so much more to it than this. And I said well –

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was you in on it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah u-hu. Erm you know I said well actually I contacted HR. And [placement tutor] seemed quite disapproving by that I done that. And I’m thinking well nothing was get - I tried the - the in-house rule first and it wasn’t working, nothing was going to happen. And that was blatantly obvious. (Yeah) But I tried that three times. Look you know, I’ll use the three strike rule. Tried that three times. And then it wasn’t running and crying every time. It was just if it had really hurt me or really got to me. Then, you know I shouldn’t be leaving work in tears. That’s the, the bottom factor basically. But it was a case of, “Oh, did you did - so you contacted HR, oh”. “Well um”. And there wasn’t a well done or er, I understand why. I wasn’t expecting praise for it, but there wasn’t any kind of reassuring act there whatsoever. It was like, oh you know you’re broke the, the old school rule. Basically that’s how I felt. So, I don’t know. It was a bit. I lost a bit of faith in him in a way. Because he didn’t act as I hoped he would have done. But I think some of the other tutors, male tutors at uni would have acted differently, and would have been right behind me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you would rather have had a different placement tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you been able to be in contact with anyone else at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ve been in contact with [name] who’s my, who was my first year mechanics tutor, but I started DT three weeks late because of the A level mis-marking. So, [name] really helped me integrate into the course and gave me lots of work, but also gave me work for the future, which the other students hadn’t been presented with yet. So that it appeared that it was smarter than I was basically. So I was more prepared for it. Which got me friends. Not friends to last admittedly but it got me friends at the time, which was what I needed. And you know, he’s like Uncle [name] you know, he is the one, to me like way up here in my estimations because he’s written all the texts books I’ve ever learnt DT or physics out of. And I’d loved to be like him. He’s like the next in line after [name] really. But I email - I emailed him and I said well, you know this is - I emailed him before I emailed [placement tutor], because I knew [placement tutor] would do nothing about it. And I said this is the situation, I think I’m going to contact HR if they same thing happens again. What do you think? Please can you just give me advice off the record, I’m not going to start quoting this if it goes any further. Can you just tell me? And er he’s said er, you know I think you’re doing the right thing, and if it’s got to the stage where you are taking the steps of speaking out against it, then I know you and I know that it must be pretty bad. So do what you have to do. And he wasn’t saying it was the right thing to do. But still having someone there say, yeah that’s okay, was good. But that could have done to have really been my placement tutor. (Yeah) But it wasn’t. So er I don’t think, I think he’s lost enthusiasm with the entire placement thing and it’s more of a visiting places job rather than a, actually seeing the students and being concerned about their development. I think if it was er being ageist now, if it was er a younger member of staff, they would have more drive about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So he’s just got the travelling round the country job, basically.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Yeah. Huh.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Erm I think I’ve asked you most things now. Last thing is some questions I asked you last time. It’s not a test to see if you get the same answers but just to see if you’re view has changed since having more experience. So what five words would you now use to describe engineering or, design technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It will be very different. Design and technolog, industry or engineering. Well I suppose I’ll have to say engineering industry because that’s what I worked in this year. Erm sexist, emotionless, very, but I think that’s the nature of the (lost words) to be honest. Erm very, very competitive, scarily competitive and I can imagine some people being driven to depression, it’s so competitive. (Yeah) And I don’t think many people have true friends within engineering. And I don’t think any of them socialise because it is so competitive. They don’t want to let their guard down. (Yeah) And that concerns me slightly. I don’t think that’s natural. When you work with people and you don’t know about them. Because I know about who’s got kids, who hasn’t – (Yeah) Who’s into rugby, who’s into whatever. And some of them sitting next to them, and you think, you know looked surprised that they’ve got children. So, erm two more. Er, very proper.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you mean by that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s erm very, well stereotypically English. It’s very…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Everything’s done by books?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Everything’s done by the book. There’s a time and place to say things. You act in a, and this is deliberately said, you act in gentlemanly fashion. And everybody abides to that rule. Erm finally, it’s pretty neutral really. There’s nothing. I mean I know most offices are neutral. But it is pretty. There’s a whole. There’s no definite statements anywhere along the line. You know there’s no. It seems like everyone’s been reluctant to make decisions over certain issues, like office layout and things like that. Who - who has what computers? Nobody wants to bite the bullet and say yes. So in that respect everything’s done the way it was done thirty years ago, apart from bringing in computers which I imagine was a great big shock to a lot of people. Erm because it works and why reinvent the wheel? (Yeah) I think, you’re engineers, for god sake, if you don’t reinvent the wheel, who is? But yeah, they’re the five words.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So what advantages and disadvantages would you now say there are to being a woman in a male dominated environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Advantages. You get to get to inside their heads. You erm, I actually understand a lot of my friends a lot better than I did do before I started placement, through spending time with men in a working environment rather than university environment. I can see what make, not - not saying they’re all the same, but you can see what makes some of them tick and, I know how to phrase things, now that things get done, rather than making it seem like a chore or that I’m nagging. And all these other wonderful feminine words that they keep using against me. Erm personally, I achieve - I feel like I’m achieving more if I’ve achieved a goal within a male dominated industry, than a female dominated industry. (Yeah) Because like at Art at A level I used to do well at that but, I wasn’t beating the lads, I was beating the girls. And that wasn’t any fun, that wasn’t a sense of achievement at the end. But I don’t know if that’s just because of having like that particular line of schooling or what. Disadvantages? You have to be very patient and very; you can’t afford to come into work in a bad mood. And you can’t afford to talk about relationships like they do or friendships or anything like, you can’t comment on people. You know even if, no matter how professional you are even if someone annoys you, you go oh God, you know oh - oh. You can’t do that because, because you’re the minority, they pick up on it. (Yeah) And then you’re being bitchy or, you get, well they don’t say it, but you get the sense that they think that or if you comment on someone having a nice tie. Or something, you know just like a general comment or whatever. Like you would to a girl, you would say your hair looks nice, if you know someone’s had their hair cut and then they notice and they wouldn’t in here. I had my hair cut, all the ladies noticed. Everybody else it’s just like, you know we didn’t notice (lost words).. But at the same time if they did notice then it could be misread. (Yeah) And everyone’s very concerned about it, and you do have to think about what you say, before you say it. And check there is no connotations and (Yeah) that you’re not being overly friendly or competitive or anything like that towards them. You have to be, basically have to watch your back. But, I think the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you still think that women should be encouraged into the industry? You said you wouldn’t recommend this company necessarily.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I would encourage a certain type of woman into it. And I’m not saying butch lesbian. And I’m not saying geek or anything else that this engineering stereotypical world has to offer. Erm and I think that, for anybody to go into engineering, you have to have a lot of self-belief anyway. But, I would say that specifically for women going into engineering, you really do have to bite the bullet at the end of the day. You have to be able to laugh at yourself. And really take the piss out of yourself. And accept the fact that you may not be accepted, and be okay with that. Because at the end of the day I will always be girl here. I’ll never be one of the lads. I’ll never be a mate, you know, it will be, I will be the girl, the student girl. I think at work, I’ll probably always be one of the girls, type of thing. But you either accept it or you get a chip on your shoulder and bring more trouble onto yourself. So I’d say if you’re determined and strong then do it, and you’ll go far. But if you have a tendency to; I mean I’ve toughened up a lot since I started uni. But if you don’t have like the initial kind of ingredients towards it. I mean it’s all very good being able to do the grades, being able to do the sums. But it’s hard to do that when you’ve got people; you could be perceived as people getting at you around you. So.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You said that [name] acts very differently to you, so do you think that she’ll carry on in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. I really don’t because the differences between [name]; I’ve got my own project now. I’m in charge of ASR Management, which is archive silicon reaction. Which is, it’s deadly, Bridges but I’m really passionate about, because that’s, that’s my thing. That’s my little baby really and it was originally, handed to one of my colleagues, [name] who’s a really good mate. And now he’s been assigned on to another project so it’s now my thing, really I’m in charge of it, looking after it. And I’m assigning tasks, and sorting out people’s timesheets and it’s fantastic. But I can say no, you book your time over there and I’m getting it under budget and stuff like that. And I enjoy it. But she’s not been set any of those tasks. Because she hasn’t pushed the boundary. She hasn’t actively shown she’d be comfortable with it. Because, you can’t give someone a leadership role if they constantly need reassurance. Which sounds harsh. But it’s true. If you sound unsure of yourself, no one’s going to give you the responsibility.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No-one’s going to believe anything you say?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s like if you’re selling a product, if you, if you question yourself, you’ll never be able to sell it, no matter how good it is. You just won’t. And I think she’s going to have to get over that, at some point. And we’ve had discussions about it, and she thinks I’m too, she say’s I’m mouthy. And I don’t think I’m mouth y- I’m opinionated. But I think I’m opinionated at the right times. And I’m not going to hold my tongue when it comes to trying to further myself. But I know the time and place to do that. But, she needs to toughen up, she really, really does. Because she’s going to get trodden on. And I think if I wasn’t here, she’d, I know this is going to sound really big-headed, but I think if I wasn’t here, she’d get treated worse than she already does. Because part of the way in the past, when someone says something to her, and they’ve upset her. It’s come down to me going up to them and saying, “You know, that was a bit harsh and ease off a bit”. (Yeah) But and there you go. That’s me. Xena warrior princess.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. So how would you summarise the placement experience?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, eye opening.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Positive? On the whole?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I could be a true engineer and say neutral. Erm.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you glad that you have done it and not just carried on?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m glad I’ve done the placement. I think if I had of carrying on, I would have had a nervous breakdown. But I’m being perfectly serious, after all the pressure of the work and. I did need some time out. And the fact that this goes towards my course is convenient in that respect. But I think I’ve learnt more about myself than engineering in the placement so far. And the fact that I can tackle things that I never dreamed I can tackle and I can go into a board room with all these big bods, and talk about structures and actually be listened to is amazing, considering when I first came here, I was like “What”. You know, what are you talking about? And there’s so many little details, you know like I’m on the train, I see - I see different types of bridges and stuff and I notice different defects and things, “Oh heck, ooh look at that”. And I think you’re such a geek. Shut up. You know when you like have that voice in your head, and you think “oh dear”. “Oh that’s going to need checking up”. So you think, “Oh no”. And I talk to [name] about it, and [name]. They laugh at me, “Oh you’re so boring, all you talk about is bridges”. So in a way, I’ve kind of taken to it. But it’s not DT. Because DT’s my passion. But, I think it’ll make me a better employee, in the future. (Yeah) And if I ever come across anybody that’s like [name], then I won’t let it go so far. And I’ll just nip it right in the bud and that’ll be done with. I’m not going to get into the, you know quite a few months of build up of resentment and annoyance and upset. It’s just not going to get that far, it’s not worth it. So, I’ve learnt, I’ve learnt lots of lessons that I don’t think I’ve realised yet. When I get properly into work or back to uni, then I think I’m suddenly going to realise how different things are. I think I’ve got used to it now and everything’s normal.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it will be strange going back to uni then? Do you think it’ll, it’ll take time adjusting again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely take time to adjust, yeah. I think I’ll probably talk to my lecturers more as equals than as kind of teacher figures. Because I’ve dealt with the people here who are like similar kind of levels of se - seniority. But I think that’s what final years all about anyway. You know you start calling them by their first name apparently, so I’ve heard. But I think I’ll be a lot more chilled out in the final year. Because it will be my own deadlines that I’ve set myself. And obviously its work deadlines but smaller deadlines.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Will you use anything that you’ve done here for your final project? Or will that be more design?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I may continue with my dissertation and look at it more from the ergonomic and mechanical aspects of this product I’m going to design, which I haven’t got a clue what it is, not yet. But everyone seems to think I have, but it’s just like a blob of plasticine in my mind. And I’m just trying to, you know leave it to form itself. So it’s a back up plan. It’s a very comfortable back up plan. But you know of course I want to re-design the wheel, and come up with something that nobody else has ever done and make it work. But that’s me, that’s what I’m like. If someone says I can’t do something, then I’ll put every single drop of blood into trying to do it. But I’m just stubborn as hell. Anyway I don’t think that is a girl trait or a boy trait. That’s just you know, who I am. (Yeah) But. You know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, that’s everything. Thank you very much for your help.
